items.author: Jimj

items.quote:
It's hard to know where exactly to rate this game, but thinking about it overall it's hard to describe it as anything other than a huge disappointment when you look at it's predecessor. Overall where this game lets you down is the main story, the main character and the constant in your face messaging from the game. Just to give you an overall view comparing this game to what came before GoT starts with you riding into a huge battle with your fellow Samurai and GoY starts with you struggling to kill a drunk old man.

Pros: Basically everything this game borrows from Ghost of Tsushima. I thought at first maybe the game deserves a higher score because of the production quality and what it borrows from the game it's built on, but GoT does almost everything better and honestly you're better off just playing that game. The game does look amazing though and the combat is as fun as the previous game generally. The new weapons don't add a lot they are kind of cool, but the way the game locks you to using them for certain situations isn't great. GoT did something similar with stances, but I though that worked better than ridiculously switching weapons based on what your opponents have. The game adds bounties and wolf dens which are kind of fun side quests. Some bounties are interesting add a bit to the game. The main missions also have some "wow" moments though still another thing the previous game did better.

Cons: The costume designs are unfortunately much worse than the previous game. The legends multiplayer mode is also nowhere near as good in this game with weaker rewards. The story is a mediocre revenge plot. Some of the characters you go after are interesting have their own quirks. Atsu is very annoying. She constantly thinks she's smarter than everyone even when she's wrong and rarely learns from her mistakes. The way the game has to remind you women are capable and men are bad over and over just knocks you out of the game. There are so many eye rolling moments in the game and it makes you feel like you're playing something more interested in social engineering than entertaining. The game also becomes predictable, because if a character is female they will be good and if they're male they will be bad or at least shown to be less capable. The game is open about it's misandry. As usual to when you point out this obvious fact people will claim you hate women, but I've played plenty of games with female characters and they didn't need to bash you over the head with messaging to be good characters. 

In the end the game had some good moments and it's built on a very strong foundation, but the direction they decided to go with the characters and story which is such a large part of the game it's hard not to feel completely let down by this game.

items.quote:
I was general excited to play this after Tsushima but quickly that excitement faded. The graphics are absolutely stunning, each major cut scene is honestly breathtaking, and I enjoyed that aspect of the development. The story however, started out with some promise but as you progress, the story gets generic and feels likes I have to complete several menial tasks to get to an enjoyable mission. The additional weapons are more of a distraction and I feel, take away from the game. And the rifles and pistols were not necessary, and the aiming mechanics were clunky. I did enjoy the open world and there is a lot of good things in the game, but when I got to the ending, the story just fell apart. It just felt like the goal was to make a multi-generational "girls' team" by the way they ended it. And I would be fine with that if it was written better. It felt like they forgot there was a main male protagonist left and had to kill him quick. I believe the term "hat on a Hat" was a reoccurring theme in the game. 
And I can forgive all those issues and chalk them to up to creative decisions by the team, but I can't forgive the decisions made on Saito and Takezo. Before I give my take, understand where I'm coming from, I work 10-12 hours a day and play usually from 10-midnight after my kids have gone to bed. And if I play a game, I like to 100% it, I get a great sense of accomplishment in those small victories. With that being said, I'm not sure who in the development team was like, "hey, you know how we have like difficulty setting? yeah, let's ignore that and make the last 2 opponents so overpowered that the players get so frustrated they quit playing. How funny would that be to have them use 2-3 unblockable attacks in a row" Seriously bro, what are we doing, how is that fun having to restart a fight 20 times or having to drop the difficulty setting to get through. For me the game is an escape, a place where I can relax and not think. The ending destroyed this game for me.

items.quote:
Pros - fun combat system - story missions are open to be tackled in any order - different regions grant you different gear, incentivizing what to do first - the game looks gorgeous // Cons - the main story is way weaker than Tsushima  //
     Ghost of Yōtei is a typical playstation sequel. Better gameplay, weaker story. I really enjoyed what this game did with its world and combat.
     Instead of sword stances you get five different melee weapons. In a rock/paper/scissor way they are each effective against specific opponents making constant switching a core gameplay feature. At the same time, the quickfire weapons like kunai and pocket sand provide powerful tools to deal with large encounters.
     Where this game really improves is its world. Completely open, this game is segmented into five different areas, each providing unique weapons and tools. Four of these areas are open as soon as you are able to explore. This allows you to make choices as to what story and equipment you want to pursue. Want spears, bombs and tools to set your weapons ablaze? Go after the Oni. Want stealth tools, kunai and the kusarigama? Go after the Kitsune.
     There is one aspect where this game is weaker and that is its story. It is by no means bad, just by the numbers. A revenge story. Nothing you haven't seen before. The main villain also has absolutely no presence, no aura. Khotun Khan was menacing and intelligent. Saito is just kinda there, and interacts primarily with his sons, who are both not menacing and not interesting.
     I like Ghost of Yōtei and can recommend it wholeheartedly. Fun game and quite a fun platinum.

HOT TAKE - I thought the story was just as good, if not better, than the first one. The story is often compared to the first one, but it was nice to have a less grand scale. The weight of an empire on you is heavy, and the fact that the first game was based on a historical event is very interesting, but they did a good job of placing that same weight of her family on Atsu. I felt much closer to the character and understood her more than Jin. 

Jin was like Superman, too polished of a character, and Atsu was like Batman, gritty, flawed, complex, had emotions, and did what had to be done.

Maybe the most beautiful game I've ever played. Those scenes stick with you.

My only two critiques: 1 - the open world limitations compared to the first one were more noticeable, even in the areas you had access to. If there was a rock, you might not be able to climb on it, whereas Jin would be able to. 2 - The dialogue & english voice acting were underwhelming. I just kept it in Japanese with subtitles on. 

Fantastic game and would absolutely play again.

items.quote: I played the game on PS5.I loved the first game despite all of its flaws. Even though parts of it were cheesy and occasionally cringe-worthy, the gameplay and the overall experience were spectacular. With this new title, however, I'm mostly confused.Years after the release of the first game, you would expect the sequel to improve on what came before. In my opinion, it does the opposite.Plot:The story feels generic and is rarely interesting. The in-game dialogue is often poor—sometimes really, really poor. I can't understand why the game pushes you to kill the first member of the Six almost immediately while simultaneously making that goal the core motivation of the entire **** main character doesn't bring much to the table, and it's difficult to relate to her. Even though she's supposed to be a broken person, she often behaves in ways that feel inconsistent with her **** main villain is simply evil for the sake of being evil. There is very little depth to him. The secondary conflict doesn't add much either.Even if the first game wasn't brilliantly written, you could still connect with the story of a broken samurai who lost his way while trying to protect his people. His transformation into the Ghost was the heart of the game.Here, you start as a Ghost-like character from the very beginning, and there is no meaningful character journey. It feels like you gain nothing from playing through the story.Graphics:Honestly, not very impressive on several levels.Artistic Style:Just like in the first game, the artistic direction is excellent.Gameplay:I'm not entirely sure why, but it feels worse than before. The rock-paper-scissors combat system is still there and worked fine in the original, but somehow it doesn't feel as sharp or satisfying this time around.Overall:It's a good game to play, but not a great one, and certainly not a memorable one. The asking price was, in my opinion, hard to justify.

items.quote: Poucos jogos conseguem transmitir a sensação de que estamos diante de algo verdadeiramente especial. Ghost of Yōtei é um desses raros casos. A obra da **** Punch representa não apenas uma evolução natural da fórmula consagrada em Ghost of Tsushima, mas também um salto ambicioso em praticamente todos os aspectos que definem uma experiência de mundo aberto moderna.Desde os primeiros momentos, fica evidente o cuidado quase obsessivo dedicado à construção de seu universo. O cenário é simplesmente deslumbrante. Cada floresta, montanha coberta de neve, campo aberto e aldeia parece ter sido criado com o objetivo de contar uma história silenciosa. Não se trata apenas de beleza gráfica; existe uma identidade artística marcante em cada paisagem. O mundo convida constantemente à exploração, recompensando a curiosidade do jogador com vistas memoráveis e momentos de contemplação raramente encontrados na indústria.A direção de arte merece destaque especial. Enquanto muitos títulos buscam impressionar através do realismo puro, Ghost of Yōtei encontra o equilíbrio perfeito entre autenticidade histórica e sensibilidade cinematográfica. O resultado é uma experiência visual que frequentemente ultrapassa o nível técnico para alcançar o campo da arte. Em diversos momentos, o jogo parece uma pintura em movimento.A narrativa demonstra uma maturidade impressionante. O roteiro apresenta temas como honra, identidade, vingança, legado e sobrevivência de forma sofisticada e emocionalmente envolvente. A protagonista surge como uma personagem extremamente carismática, complexa e humana. Sua jornada é conduzida por conflitos internos tão interessantes quanto os desafios externos que enfrenta. Isso faz com que cada decisão, cada batalha e cada descoberta carreguem um peso emocional genuíno.O desenvolvimento dos personagens secundários também impressiona. Em vez de servirem apenas como distribuidores de missões, eles possuem personalidades marcantes, histórias próprias e motivações convincentes. O mundo parece vivo porque as pessoas que o habitam parecem **** combate, Ghost of Yōtei alcança um nível de refinamento extraordinário. Cada confronto transmite impacto, precisão e intensidade. As animações são fluidas, as transições entre ataques são elegantes e a resposta dos controles é exemplar. O sistema recompensa tanto jogadores que preferem abordagens estratégicas e furtivas quanto aqueles que optam por duelos diretos e agressivos.Existe uma sensação constante de domínio e progressão. Conforme novas técnicas são desbloqueadas, o combate se torna cada vez mais profundo sem jamais perder a acessibilidade. Trata-se de um equilíbrio extremamente difícil de alcançar, e o jogo o faz com maestria.A exploração merece elogios igualmente entusiasmados. Em muitos mundos abertos, a liberdade acaba sendo prejudicada por excesso de marcadores, listas de tarefas e atividades repetitivas. Ghost of Yōtei segue o caminho oposto. A exploração é orgânica, natural e recompensadora. O jogador sente vontade de descobrir o mundo por iniciativa própria, não porque um ícone apareceu no mapa.Outro aspecto impressionante é a trilha sonora. Cada composição parece cuidadosamente posicionada para amplificar emoções específicas. Os momentos de tensão ganham intensidade, os instantes de contemplação se tornam quase meditativos e as grandes cenas narrativas alcançam um impacto memorável graças ao trabalho sonoro impecável.Tecnicamente, o jogo demonstra um nível de polimento que poucas produções conseguem atingir. O desempenho é sólido, as animações faciais são expressivas, a iluminação é espetacular e a atenção aos detalhes é quase obsessiva. Pequenos elementos do ambiente ajudam a construir uma sensação de imersão **** talvez a maior qualidade de Ghost of Yōtei seja sua confiança. O jogo sabe exatamente o que deseja ser. Não tenta seguir tendências passageiras nem preencher seu conteúdo com sistemas desnecessários. Em vez disso, concentra seus esforços em oferecer uma experiência coesa, elegante e emocionalmente poderosa.Como obra artística, como experiência interativa e como evolução do gênero de ação em mundo aberto, Ghost of Yōtei representa um triunfo absoluto. É o tipo de jogo que permanece na memória muito tempo após os créditos finais, não apenas pelos seus momentos espetaculares, mas também pelas emoções que desperta ao longo da jornada.Nota do crítico: 10/10Ghost of Yōtei é uma demonstração brilhante de tudo o que os videogames podem alcançar quando talento artístico, excelência técnica e visão criativa trabalham em perfeita harmonia. Uma experiência extraordinária e uma forte candidata a se tornar um dos grandes marcos de sua geração.

items.quote: This game is truly incredible. I believe it to be equal in quality to the first, that being Ghost of Tsushima, despite it's weaker story. That said, I still believe the story is very good, my only complaints are that Jubei dies, but I had a feeling he might, and that the Spider is a little underdeveloped, so Atsu sparing him is still a bit iffy in my opinion. And yes, I know Atsu doesn't forgive the Spider and that she only lets him live so she can save her new family, but I still think it should've been a little more earned on the Spider's part. I will say, the armor sets and charms felt a little underwhelming when compared to Tsushima, but they're still good. The fluidity of the combat is also a bit worse than Tsushima because changing from weapon to weapon is much less fluid than simply changing the stances of your katana, but even so, I do think the overall combat of Yōtei is an improvement.  That is everything I believe Tsushima does better, everything else (including graphics, art direction, sound effects, open world, etc.) is an improvement of Yōtei's end. The score, just like Tsushima, is incredible. Toma Otowa did an outstanding job and somehow made a score that could stand equal to that of Tsushima's. The characters I felt were all compelling, even characters like the Oni and Lord Saito. Speaking of, Saito's grudge against Kengo makes sense. Kengo was a blacksmith, a good one at that, he would be well respected among Clan Saito, and a vital piece in their function as he would likely hunt with them as well as make new weapons and keep current one's sharp. Kengo left because they were running low on food and resources, and because of how much Saito's Clan likely respected him, some followed and those that stayed lost morale. Clan Saito lost manpower, lost men for hunting, they were now vulnerable to not only starvation but also attack. It's understandable why Saito would have it out for Kengo, but what isn't is the lengths he went to—that's what makes him a villain, and a good one. All of Atsu's victories also feel earned: she almost dies against the Snake, the Oni and Saito both humiliate her when they first meet, she needs help from Oyuki to kill Dojun, and she loses Jubei and Oyuki to kill the Dragon. Atsu never just "gets" her revenge, she has to either earn it or lose something to get it. Towards the end of the game, Saito, out of arrogance and pride, goes to kill Atsu by himself. Of course, Jubei dies protecting Atsu here, which is one of my two complaints about the story. I believe it would have been more compelling had Oyuki sacrificed herself instead of Jubei. It's in line for her character to do that, and it would be the final step towards her redemption. Jubei's death felt forced, where as, atleast I feel, Oyuki's death would have made much more sense, been less forced, and been more compelling. Besides those two complaints I have about this game, which are minor, I believe this to be an incredible game and a more than worthy sequel to my favorite game of all time: Ghost of Tsushima. The voice actors were incredible, the graphics were beautiful, the combat was visceral, the story was compelling (I'll abmit here, it did make me cry, so it joins Tsushima there), and the score was wonderful. Truly a 9/10 game (technically a 9.5/10 to me) and so close to perfection if the story was just a bit tighter. I will be replaying this story for many times to come, but maybe not as many times as Tsushima.

items.quote:
Ghost of Tsushima had the bones of a by-the-numbers, crowd pleasing open-world action adventure, interlaced with an ephemeral charm that made the game stick with me, even though I think a 7/10 was an honest rating for it.

Whatever that special sauce was, Ghost of Yotei is missing it.

The big problem with this game is the combat.  The Soulslike combat style has always struggled when you're fighting multiple foes, and GoY prefers fields of 6 or 7 to single opponents. The target lock system is the worst I've ever seen.  Even using the optional target lock mode, the camera swings wildly during fights. It became a constant annoyance that Atsu would be mid-combo on one enemy, but another would step just close enough that she'd change her target, mashing uselessly into an aware opponent while the staggered one I'd been trying to kill collected himself and counterattacked.  Given the game's emphasis on setting up kill streaks without taking damage, this experience felt unnecessarily punishing, particularly for how common it is.

Atsu has more weapons than Jin Sakai did, to her detriment.  You'll have more than a dozen by the end of the game, 4 of which use multiple ammo types, each selected by holding a combination of buttons at once.  Trying to switch anything but melee weapons mid-fight is needlessly difficult, since you don't have enough fingers to keep blocking and dodging during.

This game uses the color-coded block/parry/dodge attacks, this time adding disarming attacks that knock away your equipped weapon. I have to find the game where this feels good, and GoY makes it feel worse than usual.  The parry warning in particular is terrible, offset from the actual animation you need to interrupt just far enough to make parries more confusing than ever, while just as punishing as you'd expect.  The shinobi, in particular, are a royal pain to fight.

And you'll be doing a *lot* of fighting.  The stealth mechanics are introduced much later than in GoT, including the ability to listen for enemies. The end result if that you're going to using your katana a lot and your tanto very little until about 2/3 of the way through the game.

The story is good enough.  There are moments that feel very predictable, but others that caught me by surprise.  The key characters are likeable (and the intolerable side character is at least a much smaller presence than Kenji was). Atsu's story is one I've seen told before, but almost always worse than Ghost of Yotei tells it.

The hard truth is that the moment-to-moment gameplay of Ghost of Yotei drags it down.  I kept waiting for the moment that the combat would click.  It never did.  It's just cumbersome and frustrating the whole way through.  It's hard to recommend a game like that.

items.quote: Ghost of Yotei est un jeu qui m’a plutôt surpris, je pensais qu’il serait aussi bien que Ghost of Tsushima surcoté par les gens, mais en fait, il a corrigé pas mal de ses défauts.Tout d’abord, son gameplay est super, il y a une mise en place de différentes armes du jeu qui remplace tout bêtement les positions du sabre dans le premier, cependant on a poussé plus loin la maîtrise de l’arme, chaque arme a son petit apprentissage au préalable qui ont toutes le même schéma, mais rajoute un côté plus complet par rapport au premier. Le synopsis de l’histoire est très simple, parlant de vengeance, mais qui est efficace, certaines révélations sont prévisibles ce qui est dommage, car l’effet n’y est donc plus. Certaines quêtes secondaires sont vraiment très intéressantes et d’autre un peu moins, il y quelques fois des petites incohérences, mais dans l’ensemble, c’est bien.Cependant, les grosses qualités du jeu sont sa beauté, vraiment le jeu est sublime, l’un des plus beaux de la PS5 et les musiques qui sont vraiment magnifique, beaucoup plus marquantes que son prédécesseur et beaucoup plus poétique. D’ailleurs, elle fait partie d’un élément central du jeu avec le shamisen qui fait partie des compétence d’Atsu qui vont permettrons principalement de trouver les différents points d’intérêts si vous n’avez pas envie de trop explorer l’open world, mais je vous conseille de le faire le moins possible ou en fin de jeu quand vous bloquerai sur les derniers restants, cela ruinerait l’intérêt de l’open world qui a grandement était amélioré dans ce nouvelle opus. L’exploration est beaucoup mise en avant, le joueur est moins guidé, c’est à lui d’exploré, il peut être aider par notamment le shamisen avec les différentes mélodies, mais aussi avec les cartes qui sont une alternative entre le shamisen et l’exploration, cela donne un endroit vague et vous devrez explorez la zone pour voir ce qu’il s'y trouve.Atsu aura également la possibilité d’avoir un loup qui combattra a ces côté, et qui va renforcé l’infiltration mais aussi les combats dans les différents camp des Six Yotei qui sont vraiment moins répétitif a faire comme dans le premier jeu, il y en a beaucoup moins et cela permet au joueur de ne pas faire que ca en enchainant les différents camps car en effet la répétitivité dans ce jeu est quasi absente si vous décider de faire le jeu sans l’ambition de faire le platine mais sinon, si vous décidez de faire les différentes activité comme le sumi-e (le dessin), les hôtels qui permettent d’améliorer vos compétence dans l’arbre prévu a cette effet, les renards, les bains thermales, les cosmétiques etc… Ici, la répétitivité sera au rendez-vous si vous utilisez le shamisen, mais si vous arrivez à tout trouver en explorant le monde, je pense que ça peut être un peu moins frustrant. Je dirais que c’est le seul gros défaut du jeu comme beaucoup d’open world, cependant, il est beaucoup plus agréable de faire ce platine que celui de Tsushima si vous êtes complétioniste.Dans l’ensemble, le jeu est vraiment très bon, il corrige de nombreux défauts, son monde est super beau et est intéressant à explorer jusqu’à un certain moment, mais reste une amélioration par rapport a Ghost of Tushima.

items.quote: Ghost of Yōtei continues the legacy of Ghost of Tsushima with a proposal that, while somewhat continuist, manages to retain the soul of the series. Its story is perhaps a bit more predictable than expected, although it does introduce a few twists that help keep things engaging. It doesn’t try to replicate the exact narrative structure of the previous game, but it shares the same spirit: an adventure with strong emotional weight, built around themes of honor, vengeance, and the identity of its protagonist.From a gameplay perspective, the title clearly follows the path laid out by its predecessor. The combat system keeps its core foundations but introduces new weapons and small adjustments that bring freshness to encounters. Exploration and stealth work very similarly to what we saw in Tsushima, while the open world once again offers a variety of interesting side stories. Some of them directly evoke the mythic tales from the previous game, such as the legends that allow players to recover the sword of Jin Sakai, adding memorable moments to the adventure.Technically, Ghost of Yōtei is where the game truly shines. If the previous title was already impressive, this installment raises the bar even higher. The landscapes are simply breathtaking, and combined with a carefully crafted soundtrack, they often invite the player to pause for a few moments just to admire the scenery. Performance on PS5 has been excellent, delivering a smooth and polished experience throughout the entire **** terms of length, completing the main story along with most side activities can take around 45 hours. Without necessarily reaching full completion, the game offers plenty of content for players who enjoy exploring every corner of the map, including missions, bounty hunts, and other optional **** final impression is very positive. Although Ghost of Yōtei can feel like a direct evolution of Ghost of Tsushima in many ways, it successfully improves several elements while preserving the charm of the formula. It’s an easy recommendation for players coming from Tsushima, but also an excellent entry point for newcomers, as its story does not directly depend on the events of the previous game.

items.quote: A cinematic Sony game, through and through, for better and worse. It has all the stunning beauty of games like God of War (and its prequel, Ghost of Tsushima), along with all the annoying contrivances of such games - gimmicky, supposedly "cinematic" annoyances like having your character being forced to the speed of a crawl at certain points, being forced to escort characters, or using the controller's touch pad to draw the names of your enemies using calligraphy. In addition, I have personally found that the lack of compelling progression mechanics, the occasionally cliché story beats, and the game's overwhelming similarity to its prequel all blend together to make Ghost of Yotei seem like an overpriced disappointment to me - it is a great-looking game, but feels mostly devoid of the magic that made Tsushima before it such a compelling video game. Ultimately, Yotei lost me within the first hour - Ghost of Tsushima pulled off a much better version of what it tries to do half a decade ago, and I deeply regret paying full price for what I was hoping would be something I could at least call "decent fun," and rated an 8.

items.quote: Para ser honesto, nunca joguei Ghost of Tsushima, então não farei comparações. Mas preciso dizer: Ghost of Yotei é fantástico. Fazia tempo que um jogo não me despertava tanta vontade de chegar em casa, ligar o videogame e me sentir como nos velhos tempos. A diferença é que, aqui, a imersão nunca cansa. As missões secundárias, longe de serem entediantes, são cativantes... você realmente quer fazer todas. Durante toda a minha jornada, não encontrei um único bug sequer, tudo funciona com uma fluidez impressionante. Outro ponto de destaque é a ausência de pop-ins. Isso pra mim é algo que não deveria existir na atual geração... Dropei Elden Ring exatamente por causa disso... gramas e outros objetos surgindo do nada a cada cinco passos é ridículo. Em Ghost of Yotei, isso não acontece. É um verdadeiro sonho. Isso mostra como saber mexer no hardware do videogame faz toda a diferença, esse sim é um jogo que entrega uma experiência digna de nova geração. Resumindo: esse jogo merece nota 10. Magnífico!

items.author: balie

items.quote:
Ghost of Tsushima was a pure masterpiece. An exceptional work in the video game scene. A distinctive style, gameplay that isn’t perfect but is functional and effective. Art direction that is absolutely breathtaking and memorable. And above all, a story that deals with a rare subject, with a thrilling plot. The hope of someone protecting their country and island against one of the most powerful armies in the world at the time! Memorable!Do you see where I’m going with this? Ghost of Yotei kept everything from its big brother but without improving it, and added a mundane personal revenge story. Sure, the cause is just, family is sacred, and anyway, the bad guys are bad to everyone, so they might as well be punished. The story and its outcome become terribly predictable and bland. It’s incredibly boring, I forced myself to finish it... And then why... Why insist so heavily on the essential role of women in the adventure ? A few simple examples:

"Warning, major spoilers."

The heroine only has to eliminate men among the six of Yotei. We realize there’s a woman, but she betrays the bad guys to ultimately help Atsu survive, and then helps her and her brother eliminate the villains. So redemption is only reserved for women? Yes, traditionally in Japanese folklore, the onryo, the vengeful ghost, is usually female, and who cares, we don’t give a damn! 
When you see how inspiring and so right all the women in Ghibli’s works are: San (Princess Mononoke), Sheeta (Castle in the Sky), Kiki (Kiki’s Delivery Service), Sophie (Howl’s Moving Castle), Marnie (When Marnie Was There), Fio (Porco Rosso), Satsuki (My Neighbor Totoro). Except in Ghost of Yotei, it’s heavy-handed and falsely subtle. It’s not neutral. It has to be a kind woman standing up against evil men. The bad guys are only men. Atsu’s father has little role except as a blacksmith. We focus much more on the mother’s death, Atsu has a niece who looks a lot like her, so the attachment is stronger. 
The only important man in the story: Jubei, dies. Why not alternate with gameplay from Jubei and his story? In the end, only the women remain, a new life free of men can finally begin... Even the wolf! It’s a SHE-WOLF! Because apparently, they have more sensitivity to understand each other than if it were a male wolf...? 

It’s too much, there’s no point in insisting so heavily, it’s useless and counterproductive. There’s no additional subtlety or depth. Neither in the characters’ emotions nor in their relationships. So what’s the point? Why not make it a strength? It’s flat and predictable. The dialogues are dull, linear, it’s as if the characters aren’t allowed to have strong personalities, I didn’t get attached to them. It ruins all the excitement of coming back and the desire to continue the adventure. That’s just my opinion.

items.quote:
I played Ghost of Yotei for 70 hours. Every hour of it was fun and interesting, but between one game session and another I didn’t feel a strong desire to keep playing.
The game world is wonderful and astonishing, especially the grasslands, but it feels a bit empty and structurally outdated.
The graphics are a mixed bag: some environments and cutscenes are stunning and immersive, while others are less impressive, particularly when shadows and reflections look muted in sunlit but shaded areas. The vegetation is stunning, but some textures look flat and unsatisfying, as does the water, especially the sea.

The combat system is fun, engaging, and rewarding, it's the real jewel in the crown of Ghost of Yotei.

The plot is similar to Ghost of Tsushima’s, but more predictable and less engaging. The best part of Ghost of Tsushima’s story was the protagonist’s internal conflict, as he has to switch from his role as a samurai to that of the "Ghost". Ghost of Yotei’s protagonist is already the ‘Onryo’ (the Ghost), so there’s no real internal conflict in the story.

Another big issue is that Yotei’s Onryo is too similar to Tsushima’s Samurai (rather than the Ghost), sharing the same immense combat abilities and limited stealth skills. This makes the protagonist less believable—overpowered in open combat and uninteresting or under-skilled in stealth.

I’ll finish with a mention of the music: the soundtrack is a masterpiece that crowns a game which, despite its flaws, is a true labor of love for Japan, its nature, and its history, complementing an artistic direction that is both captivating and emotionally powerful.

items.quote:
It’s hard to put into words what an amazing artistic journey this game is. It feels like constantly walking through a perfect painting. Those carefully staged moments, crafted by countless developers to give you that “wow” feeling, seem to be a requirement at every turn in Ghost of Yotei. It’s as if every inch of the world and every vista has been thoughtfully considered and perfected by the art directors.

The feeling of wandering through a fairytale-like myth never gets old. While the story is a bit more straightforward than in Tsushima, it feels more personal and offers room to explore the world in different phases. That, too, has been refined to near perfection. It feels natural to do more than simply check off main quests.

The main character, Atsu, resonates with me more than her predecessor, Jin, thanks to the emotional depth invested in her development.

All of this is supported by a fantastic soundtrack, excellent sound design, fluid and well optimised gameplay, incredible boss fights, and meaningful improvements to the weapon systems. Everything comes together seamlessly, making you feel that vengeful Onryō in every fiber of your being.

Could it be even better? Almost no game is perfect, but Ghost Of Yotei comes close. Only the facial animations for the non-main characters were notable for their drop in quality. The world could also use a few more random encounters, unique to each region, to make it feel even more dynamic.

But in conclusion; this is the feudal Japan game I’ve always dreamed of.

Ghost of Yotei is a masterpiece.

items.quote:
I loved Ghost of Tsushima. It is one of the few modern games that made me feel emotionally invested from the opening hour — not just impressed by visuals, but genuinely connected to the protagonist and his journey.Unfortunately, Ghost of Yōtei does not come close to delivering the same experience.Where Tsushima opened with urgency, tragedy, and a clear human story, Yōtei begins with abstraction and mystery. The new protagonist feels distant and underwritten, and the core motivation — hunting “The Six” — is presented without enough emotional grounding to make it compelling. I never felt driven by the story in the way I did with Jin Sakai’s journey.

Because of that lack of narrative momentum, the game seems to rely heavily on mechanical difficulty to create tension. Combat — especially against major enemies like the leader of the Six — feels tuned to be punishing rather than dramatic. Even on the easiest difficulty setting, fights felt less like skillful duels and more like endurance tests against aggressive AI and high damage **** Ghost of Tsushima, difficulty emerged naturally from the situation: being outnumbered, caught off guard, or forced into desperate decisions. In Ghost of Yōtei, difficulty feels artificial — as if it has been increased to compensate for the absence of strong storytelling and character engagement.

The result is a game that is technically impressive and visually beautiful, but emotionally hollow. I wasn’t playing to see what would happen next — I was just trying to survive the next fight.Eventually, I stopped playing, not because I was incapable, but because I no longer cared.

If you are looking for a story-driven, cinematic experience like Ghost of Tsushima, you may find Ghost of Yōtei deeply disappointing. 

If you prefer challenge-focused combat and abstract mythic storytelling, you might enjoy it — but it is a very different kind of game. For me, the soul that made Tsushima special is missing here.

items.quote: Ghost of Yōtei is one of the best games I’ve ever played and a true showcase of the new console generation. From the very beginning, it delivers an incredibly engaging experience that feels polished, focused, and distinctly **** combat is the core of the game and remains consistently satisfying throughout the entire journey, with excellent weapon variety, well-paced progression, and meaningful challenges that avoid repetition. Unlike Assassin’s Creed Shadows, the game avoids bloated or disruptive mechanics, keeping the experience streamlined and fun.Visually, the game is stunning in every mode, managing to look beautiful even at 60 FPS. Feudal Japan is portrayed with exceptional attention to detail, making exploration constantly rewarding. The world design favors quality over size, encouraging exploration without overwhelming the player with icons or UI **** story is the highlight of the experience, featuring strong writing, smart pacing, and excellent character development for the protagonist, Atsu. Side quests are rich in narrative depth and never feel like filler, with legendary quests standing out as some of the best content in the game.Audio, soundtrack, and overall presentation are top-tier, perfectly matching the setting and enhancing immersion. Performance and optimization are impressive, with only minor visual bugs that never affect gameplay.With around 40 hours of playtime and near-complete completion, Ghost of Yōtei delivers exceptional value and stands as a masterclass in focused game design, proving that less bloat and more intention results in a far superior experience.

items.quote: "Disappointment" is the one word that best summaries my experience with Ghost of Yōtei. This is not Ghost of Tsushima 1.5. This is Tsushima 0.5. Tsushima was SP's rise to prominence. Yōtei is their fall from grace. After playing it, I hope they won't make a third one. I feel like SP completely misunderstood what made Tsushima special to fans. It's basically TLOU2 all over again. This is one of the worst sequels I've ever played. Everything but the graphics feels like a step down from Tsushima. Which really is a shame when you think about what could have been. They had such a good thing going with Jin Sakai and his story. Why trade that? For THIS? I can't see why they would want to tell this story with this one dimensional character. It's not all bad, I have mixed feelings on Yōtei. The game is fine, even very good. But as a sequel to Tsushima, it's terrible. I can't tell you how many times I had to pause this game and sigh in frustration because of the experience of Atsu, the story, the exploration and the combat, which is much more punishing than the first game. Why, oh why would they retire Jin Sakai for Atsu? This game feels like bad fan fiction. It's like SP looked at TLOU2 and said: "hey, if we do that story in our game, we'll surely win game of the year." (Yōtei wasn't even nominated, mind you.) THE GOOD: • It controls great and feels amazing to play! • Combat is very, very fun! • The horse is responsive and feels good to ride. • The place and setting. Ezo is a perfect place for an open world game. It's a no man's land, sort of Japan's answer to the Wild West. • You can go after each one of the Yōtei Six in which ever order you like, (mostly,) but I do feel like the game heavily hints that they should be done in a specific order. • Very impressive from a technical perspective. • Atsu can get drunk and this is by far the best drunk simulation I've seen in a game. • The mini game with coins; Zeni Hajiki, is very fun. • Fast travel and load times are so instant, I don't ever think I've seen a game load faster. Seriously very impressive! • Just like in Tsushima, the photo mode is very, very well made. THE BAD: • The writing and characters. • The very predictable and boring story. • Atsu. She's a one dimensional character and a step down from Jin Sakai. • Erika (Atsu actress) is not very good. Her delivery sounds bland and flat and is a step down from Daisuke (Jin actor). • Boss battles! Very frustrating and unfairly punishing. A serious step down from Tsushima. I don't understand how they f*cked this up. • Who thought adding guns in a samurai game was a good idea? • The art direction in Tsushima is so beautiful. In Yōtei it's boring and "realistic". Such a downgrade. • I miss some of Jin's ghost weapons from the first game. • Too repetitive. • The climbing is really outdated and clunky. • The open world feels like a collectathon. • The open world is not connected. It's split into sections you can fast travel in between but you can't go from one end of the map to the other. • Atsu is too much ****, to the point where the character and story just feels unbelievable in this setting. (It's a video game, so I don't expect 100% realism, but again, this is a step down from Tsushima.) • In Tsushima, Jin became the ghost through out the story. In Yōtei, Atsu is already the ghost from the start without becoming, or earning it. • I like the music in Tsushima better. • The game honestly feels too long. • SP promised player choice would be a big deal in Yōtei, but it's not. Don't expect Witcher 3 level of morally grey choices you have to make. (It's like instead of having the option to answer 'yes' or 'no' to a question, you can answer 'yes' or 'yep'. Not very impressive tbh.) • A part of the map is very snowy and cold. Characters are still dressed for summer and spring tho, and it breaks immersion. • In Tsushima the mongols destroyed the shrines, so Jin had to climb them. In Yōtei, Atsu also climbs shrines because reasons. (They give zero explanation for why the shrines are destroyed.) • Same goes for Atsu's ghost abilities. She just has them because reasons. They don't bother explaining why. (In Tsushima Jin didn't become the ghost until half way through the game. But Atsu is magically the ghost from the start and she already has a ghost ability, because she is a girl boss and girl bosses rule. End of explanation.) 7/10 and a step down from the masterpiece that is Tsushima. Yōtei, ultimately, feels like a soulless sequel.

items.quote:
Ghost Of Yotei is a bit of a mixed-bag for me: 

On one hand, the gameplay has been polished and there are a ton of different weapons to use and more playstyles than in Ghost Of Tsushima. The graphics, overall, has improved, especially when it comes to the character models. The fights are undoubtedly much harder, especially on the hardest difficulties, and even with all the new tools at the player's disposal, it will sometimes feel unfair, albeit in a challenging and fun way.

Now, on the other hand... and I have more negatives than positives, so this will go on for awhile. Ultimately, this game feels more like a giant DLC than an actual sequel. The game feels, plays, and sounds incredibly similar to the first game, to the degree that I quickly grew tired/bored of many of the activities/side objectives. 

For example, climbing shrines: I didn't like climbing shrines in GoT, but at least there was an excuse for why the shrines were in such poor shape, and thus needed to be scaled through unorthodox means - the Mongols desecrated them. In GoY, however... it is essentially samurai vs. samurai, so why are the shrines so poorly managed? Even worse, in GoY the shrines have little footholds or marked trees for hooking with the grappling hook, as if others have been using the same method to reach the summit... but why? Just fix the bridge/stairs! The residents of the area would never allow these shrines to reach such a pathetic state, so narratively and gameplay-wise it just feels wrong, and on top of that it is such a convoluted and tedious process, to the point it feels more like a chore than a fun side objective.

The same can be said about Inari Shrines, and thus the Fox Dens... they were cute and unique in the first game, to the point the player could stomach how boring and repetitive they become. But with GoY, I was very much over them from practically the start. There is a tiny payoff for getting them later on, as well as the charms you get for completing each one, at least.

Same with the Wolf Dens, which like the Fox Dens you have to follow an animal to a location, except instead of finding an Inari Shrine you have to defeat a set number of outlaws and free a wolf or two. It was a new side objective, so it was fine until it wasn't.

I think I've gotten the point across. It may also be because GoY feels considerably longer than GoT, adding to the growing frustration of repetitiveness all for little cosmetics and slight potential upgrades to your character's kit. If there is a third game, I really hope these objectives are changed up somewhat or replaced, like with the shamisen songs and the drawing activities.

Now, onto characters... frankly, I'm overall greatly disappointed. GoT had great, fully fleshed out characters like Lady Masako and Sensei Ishikawa, Yuna and Taka, Yuriko, Jin's Uncle Shimura, Ryuzo... many of the characters got multiple story-related missions to build them up, while simultaneously teaching Jin a new technique or furthering his development into 'the Ghost'. The best part is they all feel alive, as they go through their own drama and guilt and grief, and eventually either come through as an ally when Jin needs it most, or becomes an enemy for Jin to overcome.

GoY, instead... introduces a lot of characters, and then just uses them as props for Atsu to gain new weapons and tools. Any missions tied to them usually ends up with an encounter with outlaws, and then said-side character vowing to assist Atsu with her grudge/journey of vengeance. Then, for the rest of the game they are little hotspots for Atsu to upgrade her armor/weapons/tools and little else. Yay. If they aren't one of several key characters (you'll know the 2-3 I'm talking about as they are the most important side characters in the game outside of the Yotei Six), then they don't actually matter after Atsu learns what she needs from them. 

As such, Atsu feels so pathetically alone and isolated, and the lack of vital characters and their side-plots means you're either tackling a main mission... or you're meandering about. Saying such sounds unfair, as there is plenty to do while exploring the map, but it all just felt... like a waste of time.

As for the plot... ugh. It's like **** Punch looked at Naughty Dog, asked to copy TLoU P2, and just rolled with it. As such, you have another 'Mary Sue' with a one-dimensional personality out for blood, wanting nothing else but to kill the Yotei Six to satisfy her selfish need for revenge. Mind you, GoY executes the premise much better than TLoU did... but that's not hard, now is it? Regardless, though... GoY's story couldn't possibly live up to GoT's, as Lord Saito and his punks are nothing compared to the invasion of the Mongols upon Japan's shores. GoT is a romanticized, fictitious version of real events, while GoY is someone's edgy fanfiction with an OC.

I'm running out of words... so I'll end it thusly: GoY is a slightly-worse GoT, and I still enjoyed despite my gripes. 7/10.

items.quote:
​Ghost of Yōtei: A Soulbound Sequel Sacrificed on the Altar of Woke Nonsense​
Let’s not beat around the bush: Ghost of Yōtei is an absolute insult to the legacy of Jin Sakai. While Ghost of Tsushima was a landmark achievement in storytelling , tackling the gut-wrenching conflict between a man’s honor and his survival ... this sequel is nothing more than a shallow, "girl boss" fever dream designed to lecture the player rather than entertain them.​

The "Girl Boss" Virus​
**** Punch clearly decided that instead of a compelling character, we needed a vessel for feminist propaganda.... Replacing the iconic Ghost with Atsu is a bottom-tier move. It’s the same "modern audience" pandering that is currently killing the industry.
​The immersion isn't just broken; it's ****. We’re expected to believe this girl can manhandle warriors twice her size like it’s nothing? It’s laughable. 

The writing is so blatantly biased that it feels like a parody:​

The "Men are Evil" Trope: 
Every male character is written as a clown, a coward, or a monster.​

The Flawless Female: Only the women are allowed to be competent or moral. It’s predictable, tired, and honestly, it’s disgusting at this point.​

The Actor: The lead performance is a total vacuum. There’s zero weight, zero charisma ..just a flat delivery of lines written by people who clearly hate the original fanbase.​

And above all the woke barf - a pathetic story !!
​How do you go from a complex narrative about the death of the Samurai code to a generic, brain-dead revenge plot?
 It’s the ultimate narrative downgrade.
 The story of Tsushima felt like a historical epic; .​yotei throws all that depth away for a pathetic, unoriginal and predictable barf. 
The execution is pathetic. Every beat is predictable.
 If you have even a shred of pattern recognition, you can see the "SJW" commentary coming from a mile away. It’s not even subtle.
 
 If you can’t see the transparent agenda in every line of dialogue, you’re simply not paying attention.​

""A Masterpiece Engine in the Wrong Hands""
​It’s a tragedy that such unbelievable graphics and solid gameplay are being used to prop up this woke garbage. The world looks stunning, but it’s a hollow shell. No amount of 4K cherry blossoms can hide the fact that the soul of this franchise has been ripped out and replaced with a checklist of political talking points.

The "Girl Boss" era is over, and we are tired of it. Ghost of Yōtei is a beautiful waste of time that prioritizes lecturing its audience over delivering a story worth playing. Stick to the original and leave this "modern" trash on the shelf where it belongs

items.quote: After two and a half months, I’ve finally beaten Ghost of Yōtei. I want to apologize for the delay in getting this review out. That said, 2026 will bring a lot more reviews—but for now, let’s get into it. It’s been five years since Ghost of Tsushima released, a time when I was completely burned out on open-world games. It also launched during COVID, when the world was changing, and everyone was stuck inside. Despite all that, Ghost of Tsushima blew my expectations away. Ghost of Yōtei continues that legacy, telling a classic Western-style samurai revenge story that feels straight out of 1960s and 1970s Samurai and Western  cinema. The game opens with a brutal prologue. As a child, you’re tortured—pinned to a burning tree with a sword through your body—while your family is slaughtered. You’re left for dead by a group known as the Yōtei Six. Years later, you return home as an adult. You’ve seen war, learned how to fight, and survived countless battles. Now, you’re back to take revenge. You play as Atsu, a warrior scarred by her past and driven to right the wrongs done to her family. Her journey places her between personal vengeance and a larger war between the Samurai and Lord Saito’s army, eventually forcing her to choose between her own path and her family’s legacy. Early on, combat introduces a noticeable difficulty spike. Enemies don’t always telegraph attacks with flashes or sparks, so timing is crucial. Miss too often, and you’ll burn through Resolve just to stay alive. Unfortunately, this is where the combat falls short for me. The move sets feel too basic, with each weapon offering what feels like only a single combo. While there are five weapons total—which is great—there isn’t enough combo variety to fully support them. This is my biggest issue with the combat system. The weapons include: The Wolf Blade, your standard samurai sword Dual Swords, effective against sword users The Kusarigama, a chained scythe ideal for sword and shield enemies The Yari Spear, best against staff-type weapons and the Odachi, a heavy blade designed for brutes. These weapons function similarly to stances in Ghost of Tsushima, with each being effective against certain enemy types. Personally, I would’ve preferred a single sword with deeper combo variety, like the original game. That said, unlocking weapons by training under different masters is a fantastic touch and feels like a tribute to classic kung fu and samurai films. Firearms are also new to the franchise, but they appear very late and reload slowly, limiting their impact. As expected, the game offers plenty of side content alongside the main story. Activities include bamboo strikes, altars of reflection, hot springs, wolf dens, paintings, pillars, fox statue puzzles, and Lord Saito’s camps. While these are enjoyable, they feel like a step down from Ghost of Tsushima due to changes in the map system. In Ghost of Tsushima, clearing enemy camps revealed points of interest like hot springs and bamboo strikes, which encouraged exploration naturally. That system is gone here. I understand the **** Punch seems to be aiming for a more old-school, hands-off design inspired by games from the 80s and 90s—but it feels like a step backward after how well the previous game handled it. The game also features camps and hideouts where you can upgrade weapons, armour, and inventory capacity. One of the standout additions is the bounty system. You can hunt down targets to earn coin and speed up progression. With 27 bounties available, this is a great and welcome feature. Overall, Ghost of Yōtei is a strong experience. It takes meaningful steps forward from Ghost of Tsushima, but also takes a couple of steps back—particularly in combat depth and map design. Even so, it remains a memorable and enjoyable game. Final score: 8.5 out of 10.Great job to **** Punch and PlayStation.

- Gros manque d'animation sur les personnages : sur un campement, les PNJ vont être très stoïques et ne bougent pas du tout. Dans certaines phases de combat, seules les jambes bougent, mais pas le reste, ça donne l'impression qu'ils ont un balai dans le fiak, très bizarre...
- Animation de l'eau : les vagues viennent se heurter sur les rochers et génèrent de l'écume moche en 2D dégueulasse : 2/20. Dans les rivières, le courant va beaucoup trop vite, wtf ?
- La gestion de la luminosité et des ombres sont chaotiques dans les bâtiments.
- Le vent fait tache sur l'environnement, les arbres remuent dans tous les sens sans logique. Les vêtements des persos bougent mais pas les cheveux pareil ça fait un rendu bizarre. La gestion du vent dans Kingdom Come II est parfaite, ça suit les nuages, les arbres suivaient le même sens, etc.
- Les forêts ne sont pas si ouf que ça visuellement. Pour reprendre l'exemple de Kingdome come II, la différence de graphisme dans la forêt est complètement folle, sur GoY c'est très moyen.
- Mont Yotei : Accessible uniquement via un TP après un temps de chargement, dommage pour un "open world", il n'y a pas non plus de notion de froid, ni aucune animation si tu vas vers le creux du cratère (accès fermé). Bref, beaucoup de détails, mais qui cassent l'immersion. Le niveau de détails du précédent opus était beaucoup plus élevé et travaillé.

L'histoire en elle-même est assez classique, du revu, remâché. Pas ouf, copie à revoir !

items.quote: Ghost of Tsushima is my 11th favorite video game of all time, so the sequel would have had to completely blow me away to top **** that's exactly what happened. Everything about Ghost of Yotei is better than the original, starting with the protagonist - don't get me wrong, Jin from the original was great but Atsu? Atsu is the ultimate badass. Jennifer English was my pick for voice performance of the year until I played this - Erika Ishii does this captivating job of being both someone who's very real and complicated, but also so cool she's like a walking myth. Just the setup is so good - the Yotei Six slaughters your family when you're little, and now that you're all grown up you have to track them down and put them to the sword one by one? Classic. But as compelling as the main story is, this game does a better job than any I've ever played at drawing you into the side quests and coercing you to explore every inch of the open world. Even in some of the best games like Red Dead 2 a side activity is often nothing more, but here even the most mundane chore invariably turns into an opportunity to learn more about your targets or uncover a new lead that feels critical to your journey. The combat was already pretty much perfect in the first entry but now you've got all these new weapon types to play with, and switching between weapons and combat stances and ranged options is fun as hell. And all the while everything in this world is more beautiful than anything else I've ever seen on my TV - the sprawling, beautiful open world, the colors that change through the seasons as you travel, the way the leaves swirl up around you as you walk down a mountain path or by some babbling brook, it's breathtaking. I do have a handful of complaints but they're all tiny - like the interface for checking your charms didn't have some of the info it felt like it should have on the main screen, little crap like that. Honestly my biggest issue is a really simple one - the photo mode button is right next to the button you use to heal and I don't give two **** about photo mode. So I'd be in the middle of some heated boss battle and accidentally bring up photo mode like 3, 4 times during the fight, and there was no way to turn it off or change the button so I was about ready to rip that input right out of my controller. But that was my biggest problem, so weighing that against the fifty billion huge positives makes it pretty clear - this is the best game I've played this year, and it's not even really close.

items.quote:
This is the worst game I have played for a LONG, long time. Slow, dull, predictable, the writing is so generic and insipid, the story is reiterated over and OVER..  That tree, I was burned.. my family was murdered, blah blah blah..  the characters are non-offensive, no racial slurs, or sexist derision, the Yotei Six are so pointless, half you don't kill. 

The pacing is so tedious. The cut scenes take precedence over the actual game, combat, exploration, etc. They are SO proud of these boring Cinematics that gamers really can't stand. The duels are RUINED by the insistence of breaking through their stamina bar, & the moment you penetrate it..  you go into a stale mate sword clash. It's frustrating. As is the fact that you let people go after they try to kill you! What were they thinking?! 

You can't even camp without being FORCED to talk to someone when you just want the food buff. The Skills are a joke too! You could save up 3 or 4 in Tsushima to really jump to a next level and feel your progress, but here you have to use just one at a time. It holds your hand at every turn. You cannot even fight the end boss without a contrived defeat, intercepting cut-scenes, and a predictable ending.

The songs are so needless and are never used, the spy glass you just forget about and is pretentious, the main missions are long and weary, the gambling is so pathetic that the AI doesn't even have a turn, the flashbacks are so infuriating & reek of the Devs smelling their own farts, the actors I couldn't fall asleep to any quicker, the music is trite and full of over-bearing over-used percussion as it tried desperately to plagiarize Red Dead II, and the combat is not fun at all once you realise that it's simpler to just forget the nerfed swordplay in favour of shooting everyone instead. 

Armour sets really had little to no impact this time round, the environment didn't feel lived in nor did I remember a single place with appreciation, the spirit system was drip fed to such an extent that you'd seldom risk wasting a health bar refill on any special moves, and whilst the graphics convinced everyone else that it made a game good; all it did for me is highlight all the other faults so much more. The puzzles I just don’t understand. They are neither fun, nor engaging; leading you to just look up online. 

I hated this game. I completed it, but it felt like such a bland soulless waste. And I shan't ever buy a game from this studio again now that it's full of a bunch of girls writing dialogue that offends no one and represents no vestige of realism. The man gets killed and all the girls survive. Such a transparent attempt at humiliating and re-writing history how it would transpire in their heads.
items.author: kindlerob

items.quote:
I loved the original, well all expect some decisions that are forced on you and the spareness of the 3rd act. DLC was brutal but so so satisfying. Now to come to Ghosts of Yotei and to put it bluntly it’s embarrassingly bad. A lot of the concepts are taken directly from the original and they were wise enough not to make too many changes to them. This is its only saving grace. 

Admittedly there are a few new aspects which are worthwhile. The melee weapons are a great addition and loving the bond you develop with the wolf where the missions actually have a sense of excitement and purpose. 

However the rest are questionable. It doesn’t have the same authentic feel as the original and the camera decisions that were made are more appropriate for a film. Understandable to some degree as that they want to show off the the gorgeous backgrounds but still. Map and terrain choices seem basic or scripted as a lot of areas are more like set pieces rather than something you can explore. Added to that there are a fraction of the number of enemies roaming the world, barely any combat opportunities that aren’t part of a quest. 

Another thing I’ve noticed is that you always see the same shop keepers wherever you travel too, the main ones that is. It makes me wonder why they constantly re use them? Was it because they were rushed, lazy or so theses characters can annoy you when you make camp.

My biggest issue though is the amount of time the game seems to want to waste with either overused mechanics or simply by bad design. I could give countess examples of this but settled on the most annoying 

The repetition of exploration tools is staggering, take the grappling hook. You use to tear down boards that are blocking pathways. Great concept but as you start with the grappling hook what is the point? 

Whole areas with the same or similar enough puzzle for every main mission which quickly became repetitive. It could have been enjoyable if done in moderation.

Constant interruption when making camp by pointless NPC’sEnemies being spared to provide information that could have been done is so many other less intrusive ways

Bounty targets, sometimes it’s like finding a needle in a haystack and other times they’re not in the mentioned area at all. Just frustrating and made me abandon hunting them down early on. 

Duels have lost their identity and is probably one of the most disappointing aspects of all. It went from something I looked forward to and actively hunted for to trying to avoid them at all costs. They added extra enemies, forced dialogue multiple times that breaks the flow of combat and allows use of ranged and quick fire weapons. I fail to see how any of the ideas are good and adding all of them is a big old middle finger to the original idea. Shame on you. 

The main story arc of the game is about revenge. A story as old as time itself and it’s a great way to motivate you to move forward if done properly. The tone and pacing are all over the place and a lot of missions don’t have any sense of urgency or importance attached to them. There are a some exceptions but the level of story telling is no where near what you would expect for a game of this calibre. 

It’s one of the only games that I haven’t taken the time to upgrade everything. Done about 90% but that was my limit and that was pushing it. The were only a handful of armour sets that are worthwhile, the rest are just dull and uninspired fillers. The game took about 60 hours to finish and damn it was struggle. The ending itself was predictable and just uninspired drivel. Good thing is it’s going to be traded in so at least it will go part way towards a decent game. 

I may be being too harsh but compared to original it is such a disappointment. So much potential gone to waste and it taints the franchise. Seems like another instance of them saying we know best and aren’t we great rather than taking the time to understand what made fans enjoy the first one and build on that. If they listened to feedback from to their game testers I would be amazed. There are far too many aspects that are either tedious or downright annoying that had to have been noticed. In summary just play the original and you’ll have a blast.

items.quote: Ghost of Yotei left me with very mixed feelings — and, unfortunately, none of them come close to the admiration I once had for Ghost of Tsushima. I remember Jin Sakai for the rest of my life: his dramatic inner conflict, the way he fought against his own ideals, and that unforgettable final duel with his uncle. His story was powerful, emotional, and genuinely **** Ghost of Yotei, however, the new protagonist never managed to leave a similar impact. I kept forgetting her name during the first ten hours of the game, and even when I finally remembered it, her character arc felt overly familiar and shallow: another “strong female lead” driven by revenge after losing her family. Her journey is extremely condensed — she disappears during the war, sixteen years pass, and she simply returns to start fighting again. There is little emotional development, and the pacing feels rushed.Some story decisions also feel implausible. Her survival after being fatally wounded by the serpent is never explained convincingly, and her portrayal as a respected and powerful samurai often clashes with how she appears and feels in combat. Her strikes lack weight or presence, yet throughout the story, side quests, and NPC interactions, she is constantly praised as a strong and worthy warrior — which creates a noticeable **** top of that, the entire questline for obtaining the Odachi clearly shows how difficult it is for her to even lift the weapon for the first time — she struggles to carry it and moves slowly under its weight. Yet later in the game she suddenly jumps, dodges, and fights effortlessly while equipped with multiple weapons and full armor. This inconsistency raises the question: why include such a dramatic “struggle moment” at all if the game immediately ignores its own logic afterwards?All of this makes it feel like the protagonist would have worked far better as a ninja-type character, especially considering how much new weapon variety the game introduces. Her build, movement style, and combat animations would have suited such an approach far more naturally.Supporting characters and storylines also suffer from weak writing. For example, in the mission where you obtain the dual katanas, the family’s former friend initially refuses to train her — but after one repeated request, he suddenly agrees. Scenes like this undermine the credibility of the world and make character motivations feel rushed and **** here is the main point: the game absolutely does not justify its €80 price tag. It feels like it was made primarily for players who didn’t play the first installment, because anyone who loved Ghost of Tsushima will struggle to admire Ghost of Yotei. There is very little that feels fresh, meaningful, or truly engaging — and for €80, what we essentially get is a beautiful visual showcase and not much else.What disappoints me even more is that, although I have always enjoyed games from **** Punch Productions, this time I am genuinely let down by the studio. Considering what they achieved with the first game, this result feels unexpectedly weak and deeply disappointing.

I wouldn’t say that I didn’t enjoy playing it, but I constantly had the feeling that the game was rushed: the characters are not well developed, NPC animations lack credibility, the staging feels unpolished, and unfortunately Atsu’s story never manages to move us as deeply as Jin’s did. Overall, Tsushima had a more poetic and intense atmosphere, with deeper reflections on the character’s values and the world he inhabits. It also felt like there were far more small details to discover in the open world compared to Yotei.

In short, I played the game through to the end and I did enjoy it… but Ghost of Yotei does not live up to the expectations one can have for the second entry of such a promising franchise.

items.quote:
They did it again. **** Punch, my favorite western game studio, caught lightning in a bottle twice. When Ghost of Yotei was revealed last year I became very excited, even marking it at the time as my most anticipated game of the year, but I did wonder if I could love it as much as I did Ghost of Tsushima. As big as Jin Sakai’s boots were to fill, Atsu was able to fill them and march forward flawlessly into another glorious adventure.

These game makers are masters of their craft, telling emotional and compelling narratives with a phenomenal gameplay loop. I can still feel the bones of Sly Cooper when I scope out an enemy base, sneak around and take people out, and have to use my brain when fighting strong enemies. I can see this same skeleton in the plot, with a band of villains who wronged Atsu as a child now scattered and controlling their own domains, and having to hunt them down one by one. Even more so than Ghost of Tsushima, I’m really able to see how far the studio has come since their first game, and I can really feel the mark of mastery in how far they’ve come.

While nearly everything from cutting bamboo to following foxes feels familiar, Ghost of Yotei finds many new ways to feel different. The addition of the occasional wolf companion (and her dens) really help reduce the feeling of isolation, which is impressive considering that Atsu is much more of a loner than Jin was. The new weapons introduced all feel good to use, and replacing the haikus with songs was a welcome and beautiful change. As the saying goes, however - If it’s not broke, don’t fix it. I loved following local legends, clashing in cool duels, reflecting in hot springs, and standing off with groups of foes. The little ways they improved these things here and there made the classic activities even more enjoyable to do, and once again inspired me to explore each region with wonder and excitement for what hidden secrets I would find next.

Ghost of Yotei stands proudly beside its predecessor in excellence, creating another experience that can only be classified as a masterpiece. Atsu’s tale as a lone wolf who has lost everything on the path of revenge evolves in ways I could have never predicted, getting me even more invested into the character and surrounding cast more than I could have ever expected to. This journey of loss and hopelessness with a character consumed by her own grief is filled with so much symbolism, and tells an amazing message I dare not share here. Both entries of this amazing franchise deserve to be experienced, and it is with dried tears and a proud smile I can say this is a successor in every sense of the word.
items.author: iMustang

items.quote:
It’s a beautiful game and undoubtedly a good one. However, it’s shallow, with a simplistic story compared to Jin Sakai’s narrative. The game is also very fast-paced, and there’s no real development of the secondary characters like we had with Norio, Masako, and others. Everything feels extremely superficial, even the main story.

The protagonist, although interesting, fails to captivate the player and become someone you genuinely care about or build a connection with. Even the main villain, Lord Saito, fails to present himself as a despicable character the player longs to defeat. Clan wars were common in feudal Japan and brutal enough to involve many innocent people, like Atsu’s family. Aside from the scene of Atsu’s family being killed, the game never manages to portray Saito as a truly wicked character — he remains in the background with very little screen time and never shocks the audience the way Khotun Khan did by burning a samurai alive with a cup of liquor and a torch.

Ghost of Yotei doesn’t deliver emotional moments that tighten your throat and bring tears to your eyes, like the famous scene of Jin Sakai with his beloved horse, nor does it present a difficult final choice like Ghost of Tsushima, the kind that makes you reflect for days on the decision you made.

It’s a story that fails to deliver depth and doesn’t make you want to skip work just to keep playing.

Even the opening scene of Ghost of Tsushima, with Jin running his hand across the vegetation while on horseback, is more moving than Ghost of Yotei’s introduction.

Still, it’s a game worth playing.

items.quote:
Ghost of Yōtei immediately captivates with its breathtaking visual beauty, delivering some of the most striking environmental design seen in recent action-adventure titles. While its opening sequence is intriguing, it doesn’t quite match the iconic impact of Ghost of Tsushima’s introduction. However, the game quickly finds its own voice through engaging narrative pacing and several well-executed plot twists that keep the story fresh and compelling.
One of the game’s standout strengths is its minimalist UI approach, relying instead on environmental cues to guide the player—a design choice that deepens immersion without sacrificing clarity. The interactive map is both functional and intuitive, making exploration feel fluid rather than forced.
Side quests are surprisingly rich, with excellent mission design that complements the main storyline. Creative touches, such as collectible paintings, add artistic flair and world-building depth. Combat shines as well; a diverse arsenal of weapons paired with advanced, satisfying mechanics results in a dynamic and highly engaging gameplay experience.
Overall, Ghost of Yōtei blends beauty, design finesse, and strong storytelling into an outstanding adventure.

items.quote:
What’s good
The graphics are excellent: detailed models, lighting, and landscapes create a very appealing open world.
Exploration feels more open than in its predecessor, with beautiful viiews and more freedom thanks to tools like the spyglass. There’s a large variety of weapons—armor and weapon design are well done, and some sets (like the spider lily armor) strike a good balance between defense and agility. 
The DualSense controller is used cleverly: you feel wind, snow, nature, and even the tension in combat. 
Sound and music are strong: composed by Toma Otowa, the soundtrack leans traditional Japanese, and the voice-acting in Japanese is very convincing. Side quests are “interesting,” and exploration is “entertaining” considers the gameplay “solid” and “a lot less repetitive” than in Ghost of Tsushima. 

What could be better
The stealth system feels weak. The AI is inconsistent: in stealth they behave “like statues,” while in combat they can be unpredictable. There might be too many weapons: while there is great variety, not all feel truly useful. Although the visuals are very good, the leap from the previous game (Tsushima) isn't as dramatic as one might hope, considering five years passed between titles. On the sound side, some effects could be better: the impact of weapon clashes or gunpowder isn’t always as sharp as it could be, and interaction with environmental elements (like animals) lacks depth. Overall impression Ghost of Yōtei delivers a very strong open-world gameplay experience with excellent visual fidelity, satisfying combat, and a world that invites exploration. While stealth and some balance in weapon usefulness could be improved, the game feels fresh yet familiar—and notably less repetitive than prior entries, all while leveraging the PS5’s strengths. It's a solid and highly enjoyable game, with meaningful areas for improvement but enough charm and craftsmanship to make it worthwhile.

items.quote:
This game was an absolute joy to play. 

The gameplay is incredibly addictive. I constantly found myself wanting to complete just one more objective before calling it a day.

Its visuals and graphic design are outstanding, arguably among the best is not the best, and they’re complemented beautifully by atmospheric music and soundtracks that elevate the experience even further.

Combat is intense and consistently demands your full attention. The addition of new weapons and techniques makes the gameplay even more engaging, especially once you’ve unlocked them all. Your abilities are usually tested with a real challange, particularly during boss fights.

Tt took me 71 hours to achieve the platinum trophy on my first playthrough on normal difficulty.

That said, the game does have its shortcomings. Character development falls short, Atsu simply doesn’t match the depth or emotional connection of Jin Sakai. I never truly felt invested in her journey or her pursuit of revenge. In addition, shrines make a return, and shrine climbing remains just as tedious as it was in the first game.

Overall, Tsushima offered a stronger protagonist and a more compelling story, while Yotei delivers superior and more enjoyable gameplay.
items.author: J-O-DoubleZ

items.quote: Ghost of Yotei is a great revenge story game. Unlike a certain other Japan-set game, this one actually feels like it was made by people who genuinely love the setting. It does the atmosphere and culture justice in a way that feels respectful and passionate. One small thing I have to mention is the loading screen. It’s ridiculously fast. I don’t think I’ve seen a game load this quickly. Gameplay wise, I had so much fun. Learning new techniques, experimenting with different tools, trying out new approaches, everything felt useful. The combat is very fun. The soundtrack is also great, with this slightly wild-west vibe that fits surprisingly well. The open world exploration is the biggest highlight for me. There are tons of NPCs to talk to, and they actually feel like they’re part of the world instead of just background decoration. It made exploring way more immersive. My complaint is, that I wish there were motion-capture scenes with these npcs even with small talks. Facial expressions and detailed animations make everything better and this game would have benefited from having more of those. We don't see this much often in gaming with the excuse that it's too expensive but AAA studios can definitely afford it. Also personally I find a "revenge story" in 2025 kind of cheap because it's a overused plot. This game is not a masterpiece or something innovative. But it's definitely enjoyable and fun.

items.quote:
Positives:
- Great combat system - Greatly balanced dificulty with quite a bit of variety where you can't just rely on the same approach all the way through.
- Exploration - arguably the best exploration in an open world. Great balance between nudging you towards points of interest, without feeling like you just follow of a checklist.
- Beautiful art - Maybe not the most impressive graphics or animation, but really beautiful landscapes and objects.
- Japanese atmosphere - Beautiful show of Japanese respect, calmness and history.

Negatives:
- Story -The overall story is just weak. The whole background the the revenge tale is so thin, which makes it difficult to get engaged. The story is well told with some interesting characters, but it is all let down by the premise of the story.
- Originality - Very similar to the first game in almost all aspects, and there are other games that has done these things better since then.
- Tech/graphics - Feels a bit dated from a technical standpoint. It can be impressive, but often can areas feel empty, and most characters look basic. There is a lot of copied animations, where characters or objects move exactly similarl and in a quite stiff way.
