items.quote: Honestly, this game isn't a fresh experience; it's a lazy, predictable, and utterly mediocre cash-grab. I paid full price—that insane Sony price tag—and feel completely ripped off for what is essentially a copy-and-paste job. It's forgettable, it causes no impact, and you just don't get that "new game" feeling.Agenda-Driven Story and Rehashed PlotThe story is the definition of mediocre, and it ends exactly how you expect it to. Beyond that, the plot itself is a blatant carbon copy of other games and movies. It shamelessly rips off the revenge plot from Kill Bill and then bolts on the premise of Assassin’s Creed Shadows. There is zero originality here.World Design: Where Laziness LivesThe developers were clearly being lazy when designing the world. The whole open-world map is an island, which seems like a cheap shortcut. Why? Because islands are easy! They’re mostly empty, open spaces that don't require the hard work of building detailed, bustling cities or adding actual crowds of people. The result is a pathetic, empty open **** physics are embarrassingly bad—we’re talking worse than games from a decade ago like Skyrim. It’s a complete joke:You can walk right through certain objects—they have no collision.There are invisible walls everywhere, blocking you from climbing simple **** water is utterly broken; you step into it, and it doesn't even get you wet. It's the kind of terrible, broken detail that shows how poorly made this whole thing is.Graphics: Just a Tsushima CloneThe one thing that saw improvement was the graphics, but even that is boring. They just cranked up the sharpness and lighting effects. Functionally, it still looks like an identical visual copy of Ghost of Tsushima. It’s a superficial polish job meant to hide the fact that they couldn't be bothered to innovate or build anything from scratch.Save your money. Between the abusive price, the lazy development, and the reliance on copying other people’s stories, this is one game you should absolutely skip.

items.quote:
Ghost of Yōtei
Präzision, Poesie & pure PS5-Power

Ghost of Yōtei hat mich vom ersten Moment an gepackt. Es ist eines dieser Spiele, die nicht einfach nur gespielt, sondern erlebt werden, intensiv, elegant & technisch beeindruckend.

Das Kampfsystem ist für mich schlicht erstklassig. Jede Bewegung, jeder Schlag, jede Parade fühlt sich perfekt ausbalanciert an. Kämpfe sind nicht bloß Auseinandersetzungen, sondern kleine Duelle voller Spannung, Präzision & Rhythmus.

Die Welt rund um den Yōtei ist wunderschön gestaltet: verschneite Hänge, sanft beleuchtete Dörfer & farbenfrohe Wälder, die in der Sonne schimmern. Letztere wirken allerdings stellenweise etwas leer, fast emotionslos, als hätte die Natur dort ihre Stille etwas zu weit getrieben. Optisch beeindruckend, aber spielerisch eher Kulisse als Lebensraum.

Was mich dafür völlig begeistert hat, ist der Fotomodus. Kein anderes Spiel hat mich so sehr dazu verleitet, immer wieder stehen zu bleiben, die Kamera zu zücken & Momente festzuhalten. Licht, Schnee, Nebel, alles lässt sich perfekt & fotorealistisch einfangen. Es fühlt sich fast an, als hätte man ein eigenes Filmset in der Hand.

Dann die Technik: Die Ladezeiten sind unglaublich. Schnellreisen dauern kaum eine Sekunde & vom PS5-Startbildschirm bis ins Spiel vergehen gerade einmal sieben Sekunden, ein echtes Statement für die Power der PlayStation 5. Diese Geschwindigkeit sorgt dafür, dass man völlig im Flow bleibt, ohne je aus der Immersion gerissen zu werden.

items.quote:
I’ve been a diehard Sony and PlayStation fan for years, so I really wanted to love Ghost of Yōtei. But honestly, it just doesn’t measure up to Ghost of Tsushima—and in some ways, even Assassin’s Creed Shadows does things **** combat is easily the best part. It’s smooth, satisfying, and the weapon-switching mechanic adds a fun “rock-paper-scissors” layer that keeps fights fresh. The grasslands look incredible too—those visuals are some of the best I’ve seen on PS5.

Where it falls apart for me is the story. It’s not that the premise is overdone; it’s that the execution feels uneven. There’s no real emotional pull or momentum, and Atsu doesn’t evolve much as a character. Compare that to Jin in Tsushima, who faced moral choices that genuinely shaped him—Atsu’s arc feels static in comparison or her evolution feels rushed and not as fleshed out. 

The supporting cast and villains also lack depth, which makes it harder to stay invested. Even graphically, the quality seems inconsistent—areas like Teshio Ridge and Ishikari Plains just don’t have the same care or polish as the Yōtei Grasslands. It almost feels like all the visual effort went into one region.

To say I’m disappointed would be an understatement. I still have a lot of respect for **** Punch, but I really hope they take a hard look at the feedback (and not just the overly positive reviews) and come back stronger. They’re capable of greatness—we’ve seen it before.

items.quote:
If you liked Ghost of Tsushima, this game improves on almost all aspects, with 1 exception.
Gameplay has more variety and options in both combat and stealth, animations have been polished a lot.
Visuals look amazing and are a noticeable improvement, while maintaining the artstyle.
Open world exploration has been improved quite a bit, with less repetition than the predecessor, though it still has the ubisoft esque structure for its activities sadly.
Cutscenes are a big improvement, way more dynamic and varied.
Unfortunately the story and main character, while well written, are by design weaker than Ghost of Tsushima, due to the premise. The first game had a unique story to tell and while Jin wasnt the most charismatic character, his inner conflict of choosing between maintaining the honor code or doing everything it takes to win was fascinating, especially since it was perfectly blended with gameplay (stealth vs combat) and the relationship he had with other characters (constantly being challenged on his newly adopted combat tactics, the buildup of tension with his uncle, etc). There are such moments of inner (and outer) conflict that are done well in Ghost of Yotei as well, but Ghost of Tsushima is just overall more interesting.

Regarding the more political side of it, no, there is nothing "woke" about the game itself. Atsu, the character, regardless of her VA, is a decent protagonist that is believeable in the context of the world. Her political views, whatever u may think of them, are not reflected in the game in any way.
The argument that the game is "woke trash" because of a female lead when women weren't samurai warriors is not valid either, as in Ghost of Tsushima, a game most people loved and no one called woke, had Lady Masako, a major character, who was the head of a samurai clan, a skilled warrior herself and not only was she a woman, she was an old one too (also revealed she had a gay relationship with her maid lol), yet no one complained about it.
Of course, everyone is free to do whatever they want with their money, but this is a great game, no it doesnt have ps3-ps4 graphics, it doesnt have bad writting, it doesnt have dated gameplay, its a great game regardless of where u lean on the political compass. Realistically, its probably more of an 8-8.5/10 than a 9, but whatever.

items.quote:
“Polish the stone, don’t reshape it.” Ghost of Yotei picks up where its predecessor left off by providing a very similarly satisfying and visually stunning gameplay experience while improving on almost every aspect of the previous game. This is not an attempt at innovation but a nearly perfectly executed refinement a successful formula that pulls you in and doesn’t want to let go.
Those concerned about a new protagonist not being as compelling as Jin would be wrong to overlook Atsu’s complexity and “badassery”, for lack of a more suitable term. From the opening minutes of the game, NPCs treat Atsu as an enigmatic force of violence providing the player with a sense of learning how to harness her pent up grief, aggression, and desire for revenge in productive ways to accomplish their goals.
For those myself who loved the rinse and repeat gameplay loop Ghost of Tsushima offered of raiding mongol camps and exploring the open world for new gear and unlocking new capabilities, Yotei provides a similar experience that’s even smoother around the edges with more interesting and unique encounters in between. If you’ve been waiting for more of what Tsushima had to offer in what is, in my opinion, a much more visually stunning world, this is it and then **** you never played the previous entry and are looking for a thrilling combat and exploration experience layered on a cliche but proven story beat, don’t hesitate to give Yotei your time.

items.quote:
(Review in Progress, played about 30 hours of the game so far so I will not comment on the story until I finish the game…but here are my thoughts so far. Spoiler free!)
Ghost of Yōtei is a great successor to Ghost of Tsushima and almost every part of the game has been revamped or improved from the first game, particularly in its open world design with more dynamic encounters as you explore with some great side questing and excellent combat. The weapon swapping makes for some really engaging and dynamic combat encounters which can often be quite challenging. The game isn’t without its flaws though. I’ve cleared 2 major zones so far and still haven’t come across any small towns or villages. Where do all of these NPC’s live? This is quite disappointing because this was an issue I had with Tsushima (which did have some villages but they were all very barebones), and I can see they haven’t really made any changes here in that regard. The leveling system being tied to open world things you have to seek out gives this a “checklist” type of vibe. Games like Kingdom Come Deliverance 2 have a superior leveling system where you get better by doing, a formula I wish more games followed, which also allows for more organic and immersive exploration. Overall, this is a good game and well worth your time. Just don’t expect an evolution of the formula, rather, this is just a refinement with some missteps here and there.

items.quote:
People often say that the PS5 generation has been defined by nothing but Remakes and Remasters, but I think that's only part of the picture. Something that's just as frustrating to me this console generation is the phenomena I refer to as the "1.5 Sequel"; a follow up game that takes 5-6 years to make and is practically indistinguishable from its predecessor. 
For example, 2022's Horizon Forbidden West - a pretty game that looked better visually but was a rince-repeat of everything you'd done in the last game in a pretty similar open world. 2023's Spider-Man 2 which literally used basically the same exact map and touted quick fast travel as one of its core "next gen" features. 
Fast forward to Oct of 2025, and Ghost of Yotei is exactly one of those games. A practically identical open world map filled with identically terrible time wasting activities. A combat system which adds a few new ideas that don't do much to change the feel of the game. A new protagonist and new story which feels just as flat and boring as the last games story. As a package, Ghost of Yotei fits perfectly into the canon of big budget open world games, only people seem to love this or at the very least give it a pass where they would rightly malign the exact same game from a company like Ubisoft.

To get the obvious out of the way: yes, the game is quite pretty. There's tons of particle effects and the grass blows realistically in the wind. Only thing is, this doesn't look any different to anything the last game did five years ago on a PS4. The resolution and frame rate might be higher, but it looks identical. It also suffers from a ton of the same pretty ugly character models as the last game, which don't hold up to even middle distance scrutiny. 
I've seen so many posts online of players sharing their screenshots and under every one of them there is some brave commenter asking why people only ever talk about the visuals and not gameplay, story, combat, etc. It sort of begs the question over whether or not there's anything else actually worth talking about. The short answer is no. If you played Ghost of Tsushima, you've already played Ghost of Yotei.

Story wise there's nothing of note to discuss in the positive direction. It's a substandard, bottom of the barrel boring revenge story. The thing that is interesting to me though is that this game essentially proves that **** Punch - despite all their waffling about their love for Samurai Cinema and how they want to honor it - are completely incapable of imagining any other kind of story within the framework. The narrative in many ways - despite plot differences, basically mirrors the last game. A character that is willing to do whatever it takes and resort to any tactics necessary to accomplish their goals, all while having some moral foil in their ear constantly telling them they should do things more honorably. It isn't quite as bad here as it is in Tsushima, though it would be a challenge to somehow surpass that game in it's absurd levels of ludo narrative dissonance. Jin is presented as an honorable samurai, three levels in you're taught about stealth and how to assassinate enemies. He'll express his revulsion in cutscenes but as soon as your given control again it's right back to stabbing necks. A, because it's often the easiest path to success and B, because it's just fun! It takes him about two dozen hours before you reach a point in the story where he's on board with doing the things that you as the player have been making him do over and over again for the entire game, only for his uncle to disown him because of how horrible he thinks Jin's tactics are.
In Yotei, Atsu faces an identical predicament; someone from her past who believes that she shouldn't be doing what she's doing and harps on you for a good stretch of the story (for me this happened earlier on but you can approach much of the story in any order). The only real difference is that Atsu is without any sort of internal conflict, she just wants to kill her enemies and doesn't really care how it happens.
It's sort of a positive change from the previous game, but surely the better solution would have been to demonstrate the characters shift into a more devil may care approach through both narrative and gameplay; slowly unlocking the more brutal and dishonorable abilities as they descend further and further down their dark path.

Ultimately this is the sort of game that feels prescribed by big publishers nowadays. Largely inoffensive and completely frictionless, while simultaneously without any sense of character or a single memorable moment. They serve basically the purpose as your yearly Call of Duty: make people forget about the previous entry at all costs; Become the definitive version of X game. Don't rock the boat, just repaint it and add some new ropes to the sail mast. Because even if they aren't actually connected to anything, at least people will see it as more to do.

items.quote: Ghost of Yōtei promised a snowy reinvention of Tsushima, with Atsu, a vengeful ronin, wielding a spear and summoning wolves to thwart the Yōtei Six in Hokkaido’s icy wilds. The combat dazzles—spear throws impale foes or reel in trout, and wolf ambushes add flair—but the shine fades fast. The open world, though stunning with aurora-lit tundras, drowns in repetitive shrine-hopping and fetch quests, while Atsu’s revenge arc stumbles into predictable melodrama.Controversy erupts over her "girl power" moments: she twirls her spear, and burly samurai freeze in scripted awe, tripping over themselves as wolves pounce—culminating in massacres that feel forced. (Spoiler: The Frozen Hollows ambush sees a Yōtei lieutenant stumble mid-charge at her quip, ripe for a spear finish.) Critics call it "woke warfare," turning men into bumbling buffoons, while fans see a clever twist—though both agree it’s overdone. Online memes and boycotts amplify the divide.Technically, PS5 visuals impress with frosted fjords, but frame drops to 40 FPS and load stutters mar the flow. At 45 hours for the main story (60 with sides), it overstays, ending in a tepid redemption. It’s not a disaster—spearplay and wolves linger—but a sequel that spears its own foot, losing Tsushima’s edge. Approach with caution.(Played 50 hours on PS5, main story and some bounties.)

items.quote:
I am utterly blown away by this game. The last time I felt this captivated was with Elden Ring — before that The Witcher 3 and Bloodborne — and if we dig deep enough into my gaming past, probably Mass Effect 2, God of War 3, or Devil May Cry 3. But I digress… much like a distracted Ronin on a side quest.

Ghost of Yotei is everything I could ever wish for in a game. A breathtaking, living world that begs to be explored. A story that drags you in like a cinematic riptide. Gameplay that hits all the right notes — with charming little mini-games sprinkled in, but mostly delivering on the core elements. Fighting enemy groups feels like stepping into Kill Bill. The stealth sections? They make Assassin’s Creed look like stealth for beginners.

What seals the deal — making this a rock-solid 10/10 — is the atmosphere. The way duels are staged, the cinematic framing, the visceral feedback of a katana draw… it’s pure poetry in motion. And the soundtrack? That's straight out of the greatest samurai movies of all time - literally, if you want to!

It’s been ages since I’ve felt this pure joy in exploring every nook and cranny **** world. **** Punch didn’t just deliver; they forged an absolute masterpiece. For me, Ghost of Yotei isn’t just a game — it’s up there among the greatest of all time.

Final verdict: Sharpen your katana, prepare for bloody duels, and become one with the shadow. Your honor rests beneath the Golden Ginkgo tree.

items.quote:
A review after playing Yotei for a good amount of time, kept short:

While improving in graphics and providing interesting new gameplay options, Ghost of Yotei is sadly worse than Ghost of Tsushima in almost every single way.


(1) Gameplay systems are less intricate 
(2) The new weapons, which one would think offer more flexibility, are forced onto you depending on which enemy type you fight. This is exactly how it is in Ghost of Tsushima, but in the first game it was way more natural, quicker and interesting. I would have loved to see the samurai sword skill tree expanded, together with variety weapons that are fun. But this is not it. 
(3) The skill trees themselves are also worse

The main and most apparent problem for me is the story. It is a significant downgrade and I cannot stress enough how disappointed I am they went with this. It is solely focused on the story one human being. In this brutal time period, I would have expected a bit more than just an egocentric perspective from one human. Comparing this to Ghost of Tsushima is not even possible, as they aren’t competing in the same realm. Tsushima told themes of freedom and fear, honour and sacrifice thereof. It had high stakes, good side characters that had their own agency and multiple emotional payoffs, thanks to superb setups right from the very first minutes of the game. 

This isn’t to say the game doesn’t play quite well. The new vistas are amazing, I like the lofi music mode (a lot more games should do something like that, it’s amazing for console games) and overall the gameplay is still sharp. But it is a downgrade and not a small one.

All in all I am just disappointed… everything missing in Tsushima is still missing here and the things that made it great are almost all gone now too. 
The only thing I wanted from **** punch was better late game activities and more unique enemies, events and architecture. Instead I got uninteresting minigames and a wildly poor story. 

Tsushima was a 7/10 overall and at many points of the game it peaked to a 9/10 (beginning and end and Yuna’s brother). 
Yotei is a 5/10 and I’m sad.

items.quote:
As a huge fan of Ghost of Tsushima, I came into Ghost of Yotei with high expectations. The original set an exceptional benchmark for samurai storytelling and open world design but Yotei not only meets that standard, it surpasses it in several key ways, especially in its world building and environmental immersion. From the moment you step into Yotei’s windswept Ezo fields and snow kissed mountain paths, it’s clear this is a world crafted with extraordinary care. The art direction and atmosphere are breathtaking, capturing both the serenity and brutality of feudal Japan during the Edo period. The landscapes are so alive that even standing still feels like part of the experience. 

Where Yotei truly shines is in its immersion and dynamic encounters. The world feels unpredictable bandits may ambush you at dusk, travellers might share tales of hidden shrines, and wildlife interactions breathe constant life into the journey. These random encounters rarely feel over the top repetitive, but instead build a deeper connection between the player and the land. Combat feels better than ever: The new weapon designs, and fluid fighting animations elevate every duel into a cinematic moment. The addition of wolf companions is inspired: they’re not just fierce allies, but emotional extensions of the player’s journey, adding strategy and depth to the battles.

Narratively, Ghost of Yotei continues the legacy of strong storytelling with thoughtful writing across the main quest, side missions, and additionally contracts. Each mission feels handcrafted, often carrying moral nuance or cultural introspection. The improved variability in encounters ensures that exploration and combat alike always feel fresh. While a few pacing dips and repetition in some tasks (shrines) and familiar open world rhythms linger, these are minor compared to what the game achieves. 
Ghost of Yotei is a visually stunning, emotionally rich, and technically refined experience that both honours and evolves the legacy of Ghost of Tsushima. My final score: 89/100, It's a masterfully crafted sequel that matches the original’s brilliance and, in some moments, transcends it.

items.quote:
The decision to split the combat into four separate weapons, each with only one stance, is a massive downgrade from Ghost of Tsushima.
In Tsushima, Jin Sakai’s single katana and four stances created a fluid, strategic system — every stance felt like an extension of your mastery.

Here, you don’t master one weapon deeply; you just switch between four tools superficially.
It reflects indecision and a lack of design maturity — trading skill expression for unnecessary complexity.
The result ? Combat feels fragmented, inconsistent, and shallow.

For anyone who values depth, refinement, and the satisfaction of true mastery — this alone is a reason not to play Ghost of Yotei.

items.quote: The first thing I thought was, "Wow, the fifth PlayStation can still pull this off, it's beautiful!" Then, "Well, I think I've already seen all this in the first game, so it's not surprising, plus the graphics are weak." I continued and was like, "Holy ****, they decided to do world exploration like in Elden. Just go do whatever you want, there are a couple of plot points and that's it." Then I followed the plot, and it seemed like a standard revenge story like in Kurosawa films, Westerns, and the cartoon "Blue-Eyed Samurai." And then, bam, a twist, and not everything is so clear. I keep playing and see that it's just like Red Dead Redemption 2: NPCs randomly appear, just wandering around the map, and a big quest unfolds that unlocks new armor. The whole game ends up being filled with such activities and adventures. You can simply be walking somewhere and get distracted from your goal, and a really long quest begins. Some even have different variations. Even encounters with NPCs are variable. We play on different accounts, and the events and paths to them are different.Overall, it's a blast. It's not a masterpiece, just as the first one wasn't, but it's definitely a big step forward and very engaging. The main character is also evil, daring, and cruel. Because Jin was an honest warrior in Tsushima, but here his friend almost doesn't care who she kills. Except, of course, the civilians. And everything works really well on Hard Mode. Because Hard Mode was broken in Tsushima. This is really clever.

items.quote:
I was really looking forward to Ghost of Yotei, the long-awaited follow-up to one of my all-time favorite games, Ghost of Tsushima. But sadly, the excitement faded pretty quickly.

Right from the start, something felt off. I was skeptical about the main character and the story — especially since Jin Sakai is gone. That was disappointing. Why suddenly a female protagonist? It’s not a dealbreaker, but it just felt forced. Still, I tried to keep an open mind and gave the game a fair chance.

Gameplay-wise, there are definitely some improvements. The combat feels more brutal — limbs flying off, blood splattering everywhere — it’s intense and satisfying. Visually, the game is stunning. The landscapes, lighting, and atmosphere are all top-notch, maybe even more beautiful than Tsushima. But after five years, that’s the least you’d expect.

The problem is the story. It’s flat, predictable, and honestly, boring. I never felt like I was making progress or being drawn into the world. The side quests are repetitive — climbing for a random flower you missed, or another dull path to get one skill point. It all becomes a chore.

And that’s the core issue: Ghost of Yotei feels almost identical to end game of Ghost of Tsushima, just with a few tweaks. No real evolution, no spark. The story lacks emotion and depth, and I actually found myself getting sleepy while playing.

It’s a shame, because Ghost of Tsushima was a masterpiece — a top-tier game that helped many of us unwind during the pandemic. Ghost of Yotei tries to recreate that magic, but ends up feeling like a lazy copy.

Conclusion:
Ghost of Yotei is visually impressive and slightly refined in combat, but overall uninspired. It fails to capture the soul and excitement of its predecessor.

+ Pros:
Improved combat 
More gore and realism 
Beautiful visuals 

– Cons:
Boring and predictable story 
Repetitive (side) quests 
Lacks innovation or emotional depth 

Final Score: 4 / 10 – Gorgeous, but empty and forgettable.

items.quote:
Ghost of Yokeu — A Deranged Samurai Soap Opera No One Asked For

Where do I even begin? Ghost of Yokeu promises revenge, samurai duels, and epic landscapes, but it delivers a clumsy mess that feels half-hearted and terribly overhyped.

Story & Characters
The narrative reads like a perfunctory checklist: “Family murdered? Check. Mysterious masked villains? Check. Vague spiritual sidequests? Check.” The protagonist is supposed to be haunted, driven, nuanced — but instead comes across as a cardboard cut-out with a vendetta and zero personality beyond “angry.” Every NPC spouts clichés. Dialogue is so forced that I kept expecting someone to break into a soliloquy about honor over a campfire, complete with thunder in the background.

Gameplay & Combat
You’d hope for fluid swordplay and tight mechanics in a samurai game. Nope. The duels feel sloppy, the AI is inconsistent — sometimes the enemy fights like a suicidal samurai, other times they rubber-band around or stand still while you mash buttons. And don’t get me started on the “special move” animations: dramatic, flashy, and utterly useless when you’re swarmed by three goons and the camera flips upside down.

Open World & Exploration
The “vast open world” is full of empty stretches, pointless collectibles, and filler missions like “go fetch X from cave Y so I can remember my past.” The landscapes are okay to look at, but they lack life — animals, villagers, background events — everything feels sterile, as though someone forgot to populate the world. Fast travel and map features are poorly designed, making navigation more of a chore than a pleasure.

Technical & Design Issues
Bugs, glitches, and jank abound. I watched my horse clip through walls. Enemies sometimes pop into existence mid-scene. The camera frequently locks during fights, making counterattacks feel like a guessing game. Graphical consistency wobbles — sometimes the lighting looks great, other moments it looks like PS3 midlife.

Conclusion
Ghost of Yokeu is a bloated, oversold game that aims for poetic vengeance but ends up as a lackluster, derivative experience. It’s a bland retread of samurai tropes, dressed in flashy visuals and padded with filler, with barely a spark of originality. Avoid it — unless you just want to suffer through melodramatic anger for 40+ hours.

items.quote:
I’ll be honest, I went into this game keeping my expectations low and after playing 16 hours I’ve come to the conclusion that I was underestimating this game a lot. This game is an improvement in every way-over GOT. 

Let’s start with part that I found most boring in GOT, the open world. Everything was checklisty with follow 9000 birds and foxes. In GOY world feels alive and dynamic. The side missions are on par with the witcher3, you get random encounters red 2 style. Many times I’ve met a random NPC in open world and it evolved into an elaborate side quest that I wasn’t expecting. You’ve environmental puzzles, unique stranger interaction, and many side quests come to you. Then you got bounty hunters gunning for Atsu and the world is very distracting in a good way. There are also settlements and towns with NOCs and it has an interesting cast Of side characters. It still does have “clear outpost” . “Bamboo cutting” and all that bloat but each one of them have their own unique twist.

The combat was already excellent in the first game, and **** punch has been consistent in that regard in Ghosg Of Yotie. Using different weapons instead of stances make Atsu play more likeJohn Rambo instead of a professional sword man like Jin. The combat is fluid, creative and provides opportunities to create your own combos. Every weapons have three different variations: Square, triangle , hold triangle just like the stance system in first game. The difference is that each weapon changes the gameplay in a meaningful way and there’s no restriction in using any weapon against any enemies. Speaking about enemies, the enemies in this game are aggressive. It’d be miracle ifI died on lethal on GOT here enemies attack you together, try to outflank you, don’t wait to attack you till you kills their friends. Boss fights are also varied and interesting. 

Atsu is also an interesting character. I was just expecting a generic womanFortnite character but she’s actually well done and is badass. My favourite is still Jin Sakai but Atsu is a great protagonist on her own. 

I can say from what I’ve experienced in the story it’s well paced and you can tackle it in any order. The entire game is very dynamic and less handholdy thaN GOT. **** punch took the criticisms from the first game to heart and eliminated those weaknesses. The only part where the first game is better is the protagonist and the music. GOY is a better video game over all.

And all the gimmick mechanics like travel to pay, wolf companion are very well done. I was doing a bounty mission and almost got killed, just as much enemy was about to attack me, the wolf came outta nowhere and mauled that person who was about to end me. It’s great, have been having a blast. Give this game a chance if you’re curious about it

items.quote: Ghost of Yotei ist ein atemberaubendes Erlebnis, das zeigt, wie Videospiele Kunst sein können. Die Entwickler haben eine Welt erschaffen, die gleichermaßen mystisch, emotional und technisch beeindruckend ist. Jede Schneeflocke auf dem Fuji-ähnlichen Berg Yotei wirkt handgemacht, jeder Windstoß erzählt eine **** Gameplay verbindet präzise Schwertkämpfe mit ruhigen, meditativen Momenten der Erkundung. Besonders beeindruckend ist, wie nahtlos sich Kampf, Stealth und Erzählung zu einem harmonischen Ganzen verweben. Die Steuerung fühlt sich intuitiv an, das Kampfsystem ist tiefgründig, aber niemals **** Story ist emotional mitreißend – eine melancholische Reise über Verlust, Ehre und Selbstfindung. Dazu kommt ein brillanter Soundtrack, der traditionelle japanische Instrumente mit moderner Orchestermusik kombiniert und jede Szene perfekt untermalt.Kurz gesagt: Ghost of Yotei ist nicht nur ein Spiel, sondern eine spirituelle Erfahrung. Wer Ghost of Tsushima oder Sekiro mochte, wird hier ein neues Lieblingsspiel finden.Fazit:Ein emotionales, visuell überwältigendes Meisterwerk – eines der besten Spiele des Jahres!

items.quote: Ghost of Yotei is an incredible game,  I’ve already sunk in around 20 hours into it! Right now, I’m hunting down the second of the Yotei Six (technically the first target you track, since the first one was defeated at the start of the game). The combat feels fluid, and I’ve been playing on Lethal, the game’s hardest difficulty. So far, I’ve unlocked three weapon types, which serve as a substitute for the stance system from Ghost of Tsushima. It works similarly, but instead of changing stances, you need to swap between weapons,  each one being more effective depending on what your enemy wields. On Lethal difficulty, even regular enemies can take you down in just one or two hits (usually two), so mastering the combat is essential. The parry window is tighter, and enemies are far more relentless. As you explore, you’ll find various charms that help you survive a few extra hits, but make no mistake, death comes often!Exploration feels very reminiscent of Tsushima. The Guiding Wind still acts as your compass, and familiar mechanics like the Golden Bird, fox dens, hot springs, and bamboo strikes make a return. However, Ghost of Yotei adds fresh elements like statue puzzles, painting sceneries instead of meditating, and plenty of other new **** side quests are among my favorite parts, especially those connected to the main story (no spoilers!). Many reward you with new weapons or throwable items. The world itself is larger than Tsushima’s, filled with so much to do that you’ll constantly find yourself getting sidetracked on the way to your destination — and that’s part of the **** negatives? The main protagonist is annoying as ****, at least in the English dub, especially her tone and delivery, which can really get on your nerves. Also, some of the familiar side activities like the hot springs and other returning mechanics from Tsushima feel repetitive and kind of boring to go through again.

items.quote:
Ghost of Yotei feels like a slapdash cash‑grab that pretends to be the spiritual successor to Ghost of Tsushima, yet manages to betray everything that made the original worthwhile. From the moment I sat down, I was bombarded with endless, lifeless annoying cutscenes, and none of them convey any real emotion or narrative momentum. 

The game looks half‑baked and the whole experience has the unmistakable smell of an unfinished AAA title rushed to market. What really grinds my gears is the character design. Yotei himself is a generic, unattractive silhouette that could have been lifted from any low‑budget RPG, starkly contrasting with the beautifully rendered Yotei from Ghost of Tsushima. Beyond the aesthetics, Ghost of Yotei tries desperately to masquerade as “progressive” by shoving woke political talking points into every dialogue tree, sacrificing any semblance of an authentic samurai story.

The narrative feels forced and pandering, more interested in ticking ideological boxes than delivering a compelling, culturally resonant adventure. In short, Ghost of Yotei is a boring, unfinished mess with ugly characters and a hollow, politicized storyline that leaves the original’s legacy in tatters. Avoid it if you value quality over cheap hype. Use your money on better games.

items.quote: "Ghost of Yotei" feels like a missed opportunity, falling short of the high bar set by "Ghost of Tsushima." While the gameplay remains enjoyable, the new combat mechanics feel gimmicky and lack depth, offering little innovation. The visuals are nearly identical to the PS5 port of "Ghost of Tsushima," which is serviceable but not groundbreaking, making the game feel like a standard PS5 **** story is the game's biggest letdown. It follows a tired, overdone revenge plot with a non-linear structure that feels aimless and uninspired. Unlike "Ghost of Tsushima," which masterfully blended a classic three-act structure with open-world exploration, building tension and stakes, "Ghost of Yotei" lacks focus. The narrative feels routine, with predictable story beats and interchangeable, forgettable boss fights that blur together due to balanced but repetitive **** protagonist, Atsu, is a major weak point. She’s bland, emotionally flat, and her "tragic" backstory is so formulaic that it fails to engage. The open world is bloated with meandering side quests that feel like a downgrade from the original, making exploration feel like a slog compared to more inspired open-world games.Combat, while fun, is overly easy, even on the hardest difficulties. It lacks challenge, and I often died due to boredom rather than difficulty, losing focus mid-fight. The game feels like a simplified samurai experience, undermining its potential.Overall, "Ghost of Yotei" is a disappointing sequel that fails to live up to "Ghost of Tsushima." It might have been better as an original IP, where it could be critiqued as a derivative work rather than a lackluster follow-up. At $70, it’s a lengthy, forgettable experience that leaves no lasting impression.

items.quote:
Very little in terms of innovation, feels very shallow with the new gimmicks added to the combat, but overall still pretty fun. Visuals look exactly the same as the Ghost of Tsushima PS5 port, so not a lot to complain about, but nothing revolutionary either. Game looks and feels like an average PS5 game.

The big misfire and what really kills the game is the bland copy-paste story structure, and boring protagonist. Aside from the bloody revenge plot being done to death by every Sony game outside of Astrobot the past decade, the story here is non-linear which makes it all the more bland. Unlike in Ghost of Tsushima where there was a classic 3 act structure blended with the open world, with stakes being established and there was a build up of tension to every big event, Ghost of Yotei is aimless and routine. Every fight seems interchangeable (because they have to be for balanced gameplay) and ultimately forgettable. None of the big bosses you hunt down feel particularly unique from the next and every fight blurs together.

To compliment this open world slog that makes Ubisoft open world games feel inspired, the main protagonist is probably the most boring thing in the whole game, which is handy considering the excessive amount of bloat there is in the open world with meandering side quests that are a downgrade from the original. She's insufferable and has the emotional range of a lamp post. Her "tragic" story is so routine and ordinary, it was hard to stay engaged and not anticipate every single story beat well before it happens. 

So terrible writing, non-linear slop, and a wooden protagonist, what else could possibly warrant such a low score? That shallow but fun gameplay for combat I mentioned? Yeah, it's also insanely easy, even on the hardest difficulties. This is straight up a baby-wants-to-play samurai game. There is virtually no challenge to the combat, and often times I would find myself dying because I would just stop paying attention mid fight and get distracted by anything else. The only challenges I felt were staying engaged and picking the game back up after walking away. 

It's a chore **** built on the foundation of one of the best games made in the past decade. Honestly the game would be better off as an original IP, at least then I could just trash it for being a GoT ripoff, but this is the sequel and even if the expectation was to be nearly as good as the original and not better, this game comes up woefully short. $70 ripoff that took too long to beat and left no-meaningful impression.

items.quote: Boasting incredible graphics, wonderful voice overs, engaging gameplay and a compelling narrative, developer **** Punch Productions delivers with its sequel to their prior release Ghost of ****’s difficult to find fault with this PlayStation 5 game: menus are easily managed, the interface is simple and straightforward, gameplay is smooth and enjoyable… the list of merits for this title are endless with little observations to the contrary. The game begins by engaging the player with a clear and straightforward story they experience firsthand. It’s rare for me to find myself immersed and focused, especially in today’s haphazard chaos of incessant headlines and chatter, but Ghost Of Yotei manages to draw my attention.Keeping the player’s interest is something the game does well. The world is rich and a joy to explore. Combat is nuanced and varied, offering everything from duels to large fights with many individuals. Exploration is often enriched with cutscenes, side quests and minigames, such as climbing, gambling, cooking and map fragments! Dialogue options are available and non-player characters are unique and entertaining!Ghost Of Yotei also keeps the player busy with looting. There’s a great deal of variety in apparel, numerous weapons offer different playstyles, and skills are fun to experiment with and progress. Boss and mini-boss fights are challenging, and come with backstory, dialogue options and vital consequences, allowing for a good deal of replayability. Ghost Of Yotei also provides component gathering for dyes, weapon kits, weapon upgrades and consumables. Character progression feels constant and genuine, both in terms of narrative as well as gameplay.There’s only one detail about this game that I need to make clear to you: corporate America currently has an obligation to push politics into business. You’ll see this in Cracker Barrel’s rebrand, Bud Light’s gay pride, Target’s LGBTQ kid’s clothing collection and literally any Hollywood film release in a decade. Signaling support for activism has become a necessity, after the rise of the MeToo movement, because companies don’t want backlash from disrespecting ****’s important to understand that the corporate Woke movement is pretentious: businesses care about success and little else. They’ll signal their support for activism ONLY because they’re required to, and will stop said efforts the moment they’re no longer useful. Ghost of Yotei presents an extreme feminist agenda in its story, albeit one which is, now, heavily obscured and not easily identifiable. It’s there, though: in how the men in the game (especially family members) are often incompetent failures or wicked and untrustworthy. The protagonist is the typical “girl boss” trope which is the standard for Woke social conditioning. She relies on no one, is constantly negative, men let her down and she’s the key to success at all times. By purchasing this product you’re paying to receive this messaging.(I give Ghost of Yotei an 7 out of 10 with the understanding it deserves a 10 without the politics. Propaganda in gaming interferes with the freedom of art and entertainment, and MUST be stopped.)

items.quote: Its a decent sequel. The main story of Atsu’s revenge is interesting at first glance, there is some freedom in how you want to take out the six antagonists and some cool reveals, but its hard to get as invested as Jin’s story. Gameplay is amazing, a clear upgrade from GoT and the map is way cooler  but it feels about the same size. But the real reason why i gave this game a 7 is because of the transition between gameplay and cutscenes. In GoT the transitions are smooth, makes it feel like a movie and also gives you time to breathe while in GoY there’s way too many times where you get snatched out of gameplay. If you are in any mission, even small ones like wolf dens, after the fight you will immediately be put in a small cutscene. You cant have those small moments where you clean the blood off your katana before freeing a animal or someone, you simply get put in a cutscene and watch Atsu do it. This made me simply refuse to do side content unless i got an item out of it (not including the mini games, those are fine). The only times i could have one of those moments is outside missions, when bounty hunters find me and we fight.

items.quote:
Played on PS5

All aspects of the first game have been improved upon.

(9/10) Visuals and immersiveness --> Truly a late console stage experience. Makes great use of the hardware and DualSense.

(8/10) Story --> Toned down from the heroic yet complex journey of Jinn but still manages touch all the emotional notes, telling very personal story. The villain is instantly despicable with and the game gets you right in the middle of the revenge quest.

(9/10) World Building --> Fresh take on the open world exploration formula keeping point to point engagements and activities very tight, beautifully woven across each other. Steps away from the fatigue, looking at you AC shadows- another 2025 revenge story set in a very similar setting.

(9/10) Combat --> Personally thought Jinn use of stances felt more natural, but I was surprised with how fluid the use of different weapons are due to their uniquely beautiful animations. It make the combat sequences ever more intense,  where each battle feel like a delicate dance of patience while keeping you on your toes

items.quote:
GoY is basically an improvement over GoT in almost every aspect.
-Graphically a much bigger jump than i expected (especially in texture detail)
-Insane Audio design. you can hear so many different details. from distance to layers of sounds.(DF gave a good example in their video about it)... crackeling rocks under your feet to creaking woods in forests while you can hear individual raindrops and how far away they are.. 
-Story is different to GoT but characters are also very well written
-Gameplay wise... even smoother than the first game. The switch from the stances to more weapons was a good choice. it feels more fun. 
-The open world design got a little overhaul. much more variaty and less emptyness. there is always something happening and its often something different. reminded me alot to rdr2 open world. Also how you target the main story is more free and up to you now. a bit like in elden ring.
-Performance is basically flawless too. in any mode you choose.
-I was playing it in "hard mode". Fights feel very rewarding this was.
-The only thing that i could critizise is that NPCs/NPC conversations are still a bit stiff(Animation wise) and doesnt look as good as chars in cutscenes. but thats a Open world issue in general.. but that is just nitpicking.. the world itself looks stunning.. easily one of the prettiest games of all time with a super fun combat system and an addicting open world that captures your curiosity for exploration.

items.quote: I already know this game is going to be unfairly review bombed negatively by some people for the "political views" of the creators and actors of this game, so if this game seems like it has a suspiciously low user score, check their accounts to know if the review is legit. If they have only 1 review, or other of their reviews are littered with grifter keywords like "woke", "dei", or "Sweet Baby", please disregard them, as they were only created to negatively review this game, and not offer genuine criticism. Spiel out of the way, Ghost of Yotei is a fantastic game that expands upon the game play from it's predecessor, Ghost of Tsushima with new quality of life improvements, including new weapons for the protagonist, Atsu, to use. Aside from just a katana, she can dual wield, use a kusarigama, an odachi, a cross headed spear, bows, and even a tanegashima, leading to a wider arsenal, and weapons more practical for different situations (a nice way to differentiate it from Tsushima's stances). The set pieces, inspired by Hokkaido, are very beautiful to look at, and make it one of the best looking games this year (or at least in the top 5 of the year), paired with incredible art direction. The plot of the game does have some differences from Tsushima, but welcome differences. Protagonist Atsu's family and clan were massacred by a group of samurai called the Yotei Six, and she adopts the mantel of an Onryo. The plot is engaging, with solid performances from the whole cast. If you are able to overlook the uninformed negative critiques from a certain group of reviewers, and play for yourself, you'll be blown away by this game in the best way possible. This is a must play game, and you are doing yourself a disservice by skipping it.
